articles.title: Justiça suspende ordem de prisão de deputado eleito Emerson Freitas | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão do desembargador Paulo Augusto de Freitas Oliveira determinou medidas cautelares, como uso de tornozeleira eletrônica por 30 dias. Influencer é investigado por extorsão.
articles.summary: Decisão do desembargador Paulo Augusto de Freitas Oliveira determinou medidas cautelares, como uso de tornozeleira eletrônica por 30 dias. Influencer é investigado por extorsão.
articles.body:
A Justiça de Pernambuco suspendeu o mandado de prisão expedido em 29 de outubro contra o influenciador digital e deputado estadual eleito Emerson Freitas ( MDB ), suspeito de envolvimento em um caso de extorsão (veja vídeo acima) . Como o processo tramita em segredo de Justiça, os detalhes da investigação não foram divulgados.

A decisão foi confirmada ao g1 nesta terça-feira (3) pelo TJPE. Segundo o órgão, a suspensão da ordem de prisão foi determinada, na segunda (2), pelo desembargador Paulo Augusto de Freitas Oliveira, que atuava como plantonista durante o feriado de Finados.

Segundo o órgão, o magistrado deferiu parcialmente um pedido de habeas corpus realizado pela defesa do influenciador. Na liminar, ele determinou que a medida seria revogada se Emerson, que estava foragido desde a semana anterior , se apresentasse espontaneamente à Justiça.

Além disso, o desembargador estabeleceu que o deputado eleito cumpra as seguintes medidas cautelares:

monitoramento por tornozeleira eletrônica, pelo prazo inicial de 30 dias;

proibição de contato com vítimas e testemunhas.

O influenciador se pronunciou sobre a decisão em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais. Ao lado do advogado Weryd Simões, ele agradeceu a Deus e à sociedade pernambucana.

Já o advogado disse que ele se apresentou em juízo e afirmou que a decisão também garantiu à defesa amplo acesso aos elementos da investigação. O parlamentar foi eleito em outubro com 49.254 votos .

"Tribunal de Justiça, cumprindo a lei e atendendo o pedido da defesa no mandato de segurança e no habeas corpus, revogou a prisão preventiva e garantiu que a defesa de Emerson tivesse amplo acesso a tudo o que consta na investigação", disse o advogado.

Deputado estadual eleito Emerson Freitas (MDB) — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

A 15ª Vara Criminal da Capital, do Tribunal de Justiça de Pernambuco (TJPE), decretou a prisão preventiva de Emerson Freitas na quinta-feira (29). No documento expedido pela Justiça, consta que:

a ordem judicial indica o artigo 158 do Código Penal, que trata do crime de extorsão;

o pedido de prisão preventiva foi assinado pelo magistrado Abérides Nicéas de Albuquerque Filho;

a Justiça aceitou denúncia do Ministério Público contra Emerson Freitas e contra Rizelly da Silva Santos, mas não detalha a participação dos envolvidos no esquema de extorsão;

a necessidade de manutenção da prisão cautelar seja reavaliada em 90 dias.

Quando saiu a ordem de prisão, o diretório estadual do MDB afirmou que "acompanhará o caso e aguardará os esclarecimentos das autoridades competentes, reafirmando seu respeito ao devido processo legal, ao amplo direito de defesa e à presunção de inocência".

articles.title: Hackers usaram entrevista de emprego falsa para invadir sistema e roubar US$ 6,3 bi da Binance | G1
articles.standfirst: Sistema foi invadido após ser comprometido por uma entrevista de emprego falsa. Segundo a empresa, uma ferramenta interna de IA também foi usada para obter controle sobre carteiras.
articles.summary: Sistema foi invadido após ser comprometido por uma entrevista de emprego falsa. Segundo a empresa, uma ferramenta interna de IA também foi usada para obter controle sobre carteiras
articles.body:
Binance teve US$ 6,3 bilhões em ativos de criptomoedas roubados. — Foto: REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Ilustração

A Binance afirmou nesta terça-feira (3) que hackers usaram uma falsa entrevista de emprego para comprometer um computador e uma ferramenta interna de inteligência artificial para assumir o controle das carteiras de criptomoedas da empresa.

Em um relatório inicial sobre as falhas que permitiram o ataque, a maior corretora de criptomoedas do mundo detalhou uma ação sofisticada que começou em junho, com um anúncio de uma versão adulterada de uma ferramenta de programação.

A partir daí, uma sequência de violações de segurança culminou no roubo, em 29 de outubro.

O FBI atribuiu o ataque a um grupo de hackers norte-coreano, acusação rejeitada pela Coreia do Norte.

A Binance informou que está ressarcindo todos os clientes que perderam recursos no ataque.

Segundo a corretora, a invasão começou quando um funcionário da equipe de desenvolvimento de carteiras baixou, em junho, uma ferramenta de inteligência artificial adulterada .

A Binance detectou o problema, substituiu o equipamento e alterou as credenciais de acesso. Mesmo assim, o hacker teve acesso a informações sobre as funções desse funcionário e de outros integrantes da equipe de carteiras.

Em setembro, um segundo engenheiro de software, que procurava um novo emprego , baixou um “repositório de código malicioso” em seu computador após participar de uma entrevista para uma vaga que acreditava ser legítima.

O processo incluiu uma reunião virtual com o CEO de uma empresa fictícia.

Em 20 de outubro, o invasor usou o computador comprometido e uma ferramenta interna de inteligência artificial para assumir o controle do sistema de um desenvolvedor de carteiras e do sistema de um segundo desenvolvedor da mesma equipe.

No dia 29, o hacker usou o computador do segundo desenvolvedor, com credenciais roubadas do primeiro, e executou um script malicioso para iniciar o ataque.

“Isso não deveria ter acontecido, e pedimos desculpas pela preocupação, pelos transtornos e pela incerteza que isso causou aos nossos usuários, parceiros e ao setor como um todo”, afirmou a Binance no relatório.

Após o ataque, a corretora informou que está ampliando os investimentos em detecção com uso de inteligência artificial.

Também afirmou que trabalha na criação de um fundo de pesquisa em segurança e em iniciativas específicas com empresas líderes em IA.

articles.title: Social Security just changed for anyone born before 1967. What you must know (even if you think it doesn’t apply to you)
articles.summary: Changes to the full retirement age that have been gradually seeping in since the 1980s will be completed this year and it could change your calculations on r...
articles.body:

If you were born anytime before 1967, you'll probably be over the age of 60 by the end of this year. This might not seem like a major milestone, but for the Social Security Administration, it certainly is.

For decades, the SSA has been gradually changing the full retirement age (FRA) for calculating benefits based on your birth year. In 2026, this process is set to be completed, which could impact the way you time your claim.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

Here's a closer look at how this subtle change could cost you money, even if you think it doesn't apply to you.

In an effort to shore up the Social Security system's underlying finances, Congress enacted a law in 1983 (1) to gradually raise the full retirement age. Until then, the FRA was 65 years old. Since 2021, the FRA has been rising two months every year, per CBS (2). The final step in this process concludes in 2026, which is when FRA fully moves to 67 years.

How this impacts you depends on your age: If you were born in 1960, you would reach full retirement age at 67 in 2027. If you were born earlier, this doesn't impact you. But if you were born after 1960, this could change the calculations you need to apply to get either reduced or enhanced benefits in retirement.

This also impacts those who have already claimed benefits but are still working before FRA. The SSA applies a retirement earnings test (3) every year to determine if some of your benefits need to be withheld due to the size of your income. This calculation, again, hinges on FRA so the move could expose you to a little extra benefits withheld.

If all this sounds confusing and convoluted, you're not alone.

Only 21% of seniors surveyed by Nationwide (4) in 2025 were able to correctly identify their FRA. When asked about all the factors that determine their maximum benefit in retirement, only 8% answered all five correctly. Simply put, there's a wide knowledge gap and an easy way to fix it.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off | TechCrunch
articles.summary: CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI, which makes AI agent observability software, and Dreadnode, which helps companies automate AI security testing.
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale.

CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI , which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode , which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live.

The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal .

The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams.

CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market . It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage.

The company has itself been building detection and response controls , dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings.

Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product , to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations.

Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far.

articles.title: 7 holiday shopping scams to watch for this season
articles.summary: Black Friday deals are already drawing scammers who use fake delivery notices and gift card payment requests to steal your personal financial information.
articles.body: Black Friday is still weeks away, but the holiday shopping season is already picking up. Stores are promoting early deals, our inboxes are filling with sales emails, and chances are you're already thinking about gifts for family and friends. Scammers are getting an early start, too. Holiday shopping scams are designed to blend in with legitimate promotions and messages. A tempting discount could lead to a fake online store. A delivery alert might ask you to confirm your address or pay a small fee. And an email about a problem with your order could be an attempt to steal your payment information. The tricky part is that these messages often arrive when you're already looking for deals or expecting packages. Before you click or enter your credit card information, here are seven holiday shopping scams to watch for and simple ways to protect yourself. DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay, plus a downloadable checklist, now at CyberGuyLive.com. Why holiday shopping gives scammers an opening During the holidays, it is normal to receive messages from unfamiliar stores. You may also be expecting several deliveries at once. Meanwhile, sales and shipping deadlines create pressure to act quickly. Scammers take advantage of those distractions. A fake message becomes more convincing when it matches something you are already expecting. That's why one of the best ways to avoid holiday shopping scams is to verify unexpected messages through a company's official website or app rather than responding directly. The deal that's too good to be true You see a social media ad for a name-brand coat, popular gadget or designer handbag at 80% off. The photos look professional, and a countdown clock warns that the deal is about to expire. Big discounts happen during the holidays. However, unusually low prices on popular merchandise can signal a scam. Some fake stores collect your payment and send nothing. Others deliver cheap counterfeits or products that look nothing like the advertisement. How to protect yourself: The Federal Trade Commission warns that scammers frequently use social media advertisements featuring popular products at unusually low prices. The copycat online store Fake shopping websites can look remarkably convincing. Scammers copy brand logos, product photography and website layouts to make their stores appear legitimate. Sometimes, the biggest clue is hiding in the website address. A fake store might add words such as "outlet" or "sale" to a familiar brand name. Others use subtle misspellings or unfamiliar web addresses. Warning signs to check: One important detail: A padlock icon or HTTPS connection does not guarantee that a shopping website is legitimate. It means the connection is encrypted. Scammers can use encrypted websites, too. When in doubt, type the retailer's official address into your browser or open its trusted app. The fake delivery notice "Your package could not be delivered. Please confirm your address." Messages like this appear through text messages and emails, often claiming to come from the U.S. Postal Service, UPS or FedEx. Because you may have packages on the way, the message can seem believable. Scammers frequently direct you to a fake tracking page. There, they may ask you to enter your address, credit card number or other personal information. Some demand a small redelivery fee. How to protect yourself: The Postal Service confirms that it does not charge a fee for redelivery. If a text claims you must pay USPS to receive your package again, treat it as a warning sign. The problem with your order email Another common scam involves an email claiming that your payment failed, your shopping account has been locked or a purchase needs immediate confirmation. Some messages go further. They claim someone made an expensive purchase using your account and provide a phone number to call if you want to cancel it. That number may connect you directly to a scammer. Once you call, the person may request your credit card information, ask for a one-time verification code or pressure you into installing remote-access software. How to protect yourself: If you cannot verify the message through your account, contact the company's customer service department using contact information from its official website. The gift card payment request Gift cards make convenient holiday presents. Unfortunately, scammers also like them because the money can be difficult to recover once the card numbers and PINs are shared. A scammer may pretend to be a seller, employer or family member who urgently needs financial help. Some even claim to represent government agencies or utility companies. How to protect yourself: A legitimate company might sell gift cards or accept its own gift cards for purchases. However, demands to buy gift cards and send someone the card numbers or PINs are strong signs of fraud. The charity appeal that pulls at your heart The holidays are a popular time for charitable giving. Scammers know that emotional appeals can encourage people to donate quickly. Fake charities may use names that resemble familiar organizations. Others take advantage of natural disasters or heartbreaking stories to solicit donations. Some scammers impersonate legitimate charities and direct donations to fraudulent payment pages. How to protect yourself: You can also consult the FTC's charity guidance before donating. CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED The marketplace bargain that disappears Online marketplaces and local resale groups can be useful places to find holiday bargains. However, they also attract scammers posing as legitimate sellers. A seller might advertise a popular item at an unusually low price, then demand payment before you can inspect it. Others try to move conversations away from the marketplace to avoid its protections. Fake payment confirmations and requests for additional shipping fees are other warning signs. How to protect yourself: Remember that not every marketplace provides buyer protection. Check its policies rather than assuming it will refund a fraudulent purchase. Safer checkout habits for the holiday season Avoiding holiday shopping scams starts with a few simple habits. These precautions can help protect your finances and personal information. These habits help reduce your risk even when an advertisement or shopping website looks legitimate. What to do if you clicked a shopping scam Even careful shoppers can encounter convincing scams. The important thing is to respond based on what actually happened. If you only opened a suspicious link Simply opening a webpage does not automatically mean your accounts have been compromised. If you entered your password or personal information If you sent money to a scammer Acting quickly can improve your chances of limiting the damage. How security software can help protect holiday shoppers Good habits are your first line of defense, but nobody spots every scam every time, especially during the busy holiday season. That's where reliable security software can provide an extra layer of protection. I recommend using strong antivirus software that helps detect suspicious websites, phishing attempts and malicious links before they put your personal information at risk. Look for software that offers real-time protection against viruses, malware, spyware and ransomware. Some security solutions also include scam detection tools that can help identify fraudulent text messages, fake shopping websites and suspicious links. These features are particularly useful when scammers impersonate familiar retailers or delivery companies. A built-in password manager is another valuable feature. It can generate and securely store strong, unique passwords for your shopping accounts. That helps reduce the risk of someone accessing multiple accounts if one password is compromised. AI-powered scams are also becoming more convincing. Fake celebrity endorsements, manipulated videos and fraudulent holiday giveaways can make questionable offers appear legitimate. Some security products now include AI-powered scam detection and deepfake detection tools to help identify certain types of manipulated content. However, these capabilities vary by product, device and platform. While security software cannot stop every scam, combining it with secure payment methods, account alerts and careful shopping habits can help protect your money and personal information throughout the holiday season. But I've learned that the best way to avoid getting scammed is to be a little skeptical when something looks unusually attractive or demands an immediate response. Scammers are getting better at copying familiar stores and creating convincing messages. They're also using AI to make fraudulent offers look more believable. That's why I recommend checking purchases directly through retailers you trust and using security tools that can help flag suspicious activity. A few extra seconds of checking could save you a lot of trouble. The holidays should be about enjoying time with the people you care about, not cleaning up after a scam. articles.title: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.summary: Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
articles.body: It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day. The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years. Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.” For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives, freezing charging infrastructure funding, and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent. [Media: Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor. While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism. Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want. Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher. Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market. In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.

articles.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Cybersecurity experts have long warned of the persistent and patient threat from North Korea's long-running hacks. The world's largest crypto exchange was still caught off-guard.
articles.body:
Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop.

Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months.

This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network.

The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program.

In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware.

That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto.

Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft.

The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems.

These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.

By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.”

But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention.

While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise.

A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack.

The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident.

The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history.

articles.title: Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
articles.summary: Edited photos of Jeff Bezos and Jason Statham are being shared online that make the two men look like they’ve had hair transplants.
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. However, there are some images of the two men circulating around X, Threads, and Bluesky in which they both have substantially more hair than their usual shaved look, which in Bezos’ case appears to be very freshly transplanted. It’s all just photo editing fakery, AI or otherwise. It’s unclear how viral these posts are, but they’re prevalent enough that a few members of the Verge team have encountered them in their social media feeds. Some people who shared them claimed (or were seemingly fooled into believing) that Bezos and Statham had undergone hair transplant surgery. Generative AI tools have made this kind of photo manipulation or outright creation more accessible and convincing, and because AI labeling solutions on social media broadly suck at flagging this fakery, it’s easy to be misled unless you’re wary of everything you see online. In a world where social media shitposters can turn engagement into a revenue stream, they’re not going to stop churning out attention-grabbing fabricated nonsense anytime soon. We don’t know if AI tools were used to make the follicled Bezos and Statham edits — none of the images I tested flagged for Content Credentials or SynthID markers. We also can’t fully establish when they were first posted or who made them, but they are definitely fake, and it only took me a couple of minutes to confirm it. In both cases, I ran the photos through Google’s reverse image search tool. For the Bezos debunk, I found photographs of him in a similar background environment and wearing the exact same outfit (with, yes, no hair) that included a watermarked image credit at the bottom left. Searching for the credit then led me to the original photographs in their unaltered state, which were taken in 2023. Finding the original tressless images of Statham was even easier — the reverse image search immediately surfaced watermarked versions of the originals, which were snapped by a paparazzo in 2011. [Image: Both of the original photos were actually taken on the same day, at around the same time, but anything for clicks, right? There’s other evidence too if you know what to look for. The main flag is that it’s probably impossible for Bezos and Statham to be realistic candidates for hair replacement surgery anyway; it requires you to have enough “donor” hair to sacrifice from the back and sides of your head to then replant closer to your desired hairline. You can technically take it from other places (or even other people), but doing so is incredibly rare due to undesirable results and rejection concerns. Transplant patients also typically experience some pretty dramatic facial swelling for the first week or so, which Bezos shows no signs of. Wigs, toupees, and other hair systems can also be used as nonpermanent hair restoration solutions, but as someone who used to make and install them professionally, it would be an astounding whoopsie for someone as rich and connected as Bezos to go this route and still end up looking like a Chia Pet. This isn’t the first time photo-manipulated fakery has fooled people across social media, and with ongoing generative AI advancements, it probably won’t be the last. Previous incidents gave us the viral swagged-out pope, and recent trends have seen paparazzi photographs of celebrities like Callum Turner, Harry Styles, and Noah Schnapp being manipulated to remove their shirts. These kinds of edits are typically designed to rack up likes, reposts, and other engagement — they play into our fascination with celebrities’ lives with fabricated situations that are just outlandish enough to be believable, grab our attention, and be shared around as the latest hot gossip by those who are fooled, or who simply don’t care to verify the facts. If you’re ever unsure if there’s fakery afoot with images of famous faces, just remember that most of the convincing edits (AI or otherwise) are based on real photos that you can hunt down to verify the original source.

articles.title: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Cybersecurity-focused Ballistic Ventures is seeking to raise $360 million for a new flagship fund and another $130 million for a separate investment vehicle.
articles.body:
Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings.

The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing.

The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them.

Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies, including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks , and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike , alongside startups such as Armadin , GetReal , Nudge Security, and Oligo Security.

Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said.

In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount.

U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said.

Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged.

Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans.

One X user called it "the most brutal ratio in the history of this site." Another wrote that Vice-President JD Vance "just got cooked into oblivion."

It all stems from a Vance X post , on the eve of the midterms, that promoted a list of supposed Trump administration achievements in New York. The list includes lowering the city's crime rates, a drop in shootings and the state's murder count, preserving wages and jobs, and delivering hundreds of billions in tech investments.

articles.standfirst: Yan Lopes (Podemos) afirmou que equipe jurídica avalia medidas antes da sessão da Câmara, marcada para terça-feira (10). Comissão Processante recomendou a cassação do mandato por suposto uso irregular de R$ 2,1 milhões.
articles.summary: Prefeito de Caçapava Yan Lopes afirma que verba de R$ 2,1 milhões foi usada para baratear passagens, enquanto a Câmara avalia pedido de cassação do seu mandato.
articles.body:
Prefeito de Caçapava nega irregularidades e diz que uso de verba do transporte foi investimento em política pública — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

O prefeito de Caçapava , Yan Lopes (Podemos), negou ter cometido irregularidades no uso de R$ 2,1 milhões do Fundo Municipal de Transporte e Trânsito. O relatório final da Comissão Processante, divulgado nesta terça-feira (3), recomendou a cassação do mandato do chefe do Executivo .

Em entrevista à TV Vanguarda , nesta quarta-feira (4), o prefeito defendeu a aplicação do dinheiro no transporte público e afirmou que a equipe jurídica avalia medidas antes da votação na Câmara.

“Essas leis dão pra gente diretrizes de como investir o recurso do fundo de transporte. Se a gente falar que investir em transporte público, baratear a passagem e modernizar a frota não é investimento em política pública de transporte, eu não sei mais o que é”, afirmou.

Yan disse que recebeu uma versão digital do relatório pelo celular e que os advogados analisam a possibilidade de entrar com uma ação antes da sessão que vai discutir o documento.

A denúncia que deu origem ao processo aponta que o prefeito teria usado recursos arrecadados com multas de trânsito para subsidiar parte do valor das passagens de ônibus. Segundo os denunciantes, o artigo 320 do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro determina que esse dinheiro seja aplicado exclusivamente em ações relacionadas ao trânsito.

Além do uso dos recursos, a comissão também investigou se Yan deixou de responder a requerimentos aprovados pelos vereadores que pediam informações sobre a aplicação do dinheiro do fundo. O prefeito negou a acusação.

O presidente da Câmara de Caçapava, vereador Adilson Henrique (PL), marcou para a próxima terça-feira (10), às 9h, a sessão de leitura e votação do relatório final da Comissão Processante.

O documento tem 78 páginas e foi assinado pelos três integrantes da comissão: Fran Miranda (PL), presidente; Dani Galdino (Republicanos); e Pablo Fernandes (DC).

A comissão considerou procedentes as acusações e recomendou que o plenário decida pela cassação do mandato por infrações político-administrativas. A decisão cabe aos vereadores, e são necessários pelo menos oito votos favoráveis, entre os 11 parlamentares da Casa, para que o prefeito perca o cargo.

Em entrevista à TV Vanguarda , Fran Miranda afirmou que os trabalhos foram conduzidos com responsabilidade e transparência.

O caso começou a ser analisado pela Câmara após uma denúncia apresentada no início de agosto por Eugênio Pinto de Freitas Filho, marido da vice-prefeita Juliana Freitas (Podemos), e outras três pessoas.

articles.title: Wall Street reacts to the stunning election day Blue Wave: winners, losers and those in between
articles.summary: The views on the markets begin to trickle in post mid-term election Blue Wave.
articles.body:
Let the picking of winners and losers begin for Wall Street following the stunning Democratic blue wave that erupted on Election Day late Tuesday.

A powerful Democratic surge swept across the nation on Election Day, securing majorities in both chambers of Congress in a strong rebuke of President Donald Trump's handling of the economy.

Democrats flipped key Senate seats in states including Texas, Kansas, North Carolina and Ohio to reclaim the upper chamber. The party also crossed the 218-seat threshold to capture the House.

Gubernatorial races delivered landmark milestones as well, including Keisha Lance Bottoms winning in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa securing a win in Texas.

The sweeping victories across federal and state levels mark a decisive shift in the national balance of power and could have implications for everything from AI stock darlings like Nvidia ( NVDA ) to the small-cap Russell 2000.

Here are several early Wall Street reactions.

"The overnight price action suggested to us that the election results are unlikely to halt the rotation in leadership in the US equity market that's been underway recently from big cap Growth to small caps and non-TIMT related sectors. Russell 2000 futures, one of the destinations in the rotation trade, outperformed Nasdaq 100 futures and the S&P 500 overnight. We do see the decisive margins in both chambers as a positive for equity markets from the perspective of uncertainty being removed. Even if certain Senate seats are close or the results are challenged, that process is unlikely to alter the balance of power. We still struggle to support the idea that the election will be a major clearing event for markets, however, given the absence of the usual turbulence in the US equity market around the election so far. S&P 500 gains in the years that follow midterms tend to be sub-trend (6.2% on average) in years that didn't see a down 3Q or down 4Q in the midterm year itself." -RBC Capital Markets strategist Lori Calvasina

"Names to Play Defense – APH, ANET, AAPL, CSCO & MSI: 1) Amphenol ( APH ) is our diversified way to retain AI exposure: higher signal, power, and optical content sit alongside strength in defense, commercial aerospace and, industrial, reducing dependence on any single AI architecture or customer cohort. If things go into a recession, this is the name to own given its ability to navigate historical demand volatility better than most other companies. 2) Arista Networks ( ANET ) is our quality AI/networking expression, with exposure spanning back-end AI, front-end and campus deployments; the key debate remains supply execution and revenue conversion against a constructive demand backdrop. Not a cheap stock we concede, but the highest quality asset from a margin perspective. Plenty of growth across front-end cloud, campus, and new customer wins (GOOG, etc.) to help sustain growth. 3) Apple ( AAPL ) offers a different earnings driver through iPhone mix/pricing and Services rather than data-center construction; our work points to resilient demand, with gross-margin recovery and price elasticity the key tests. This is THE name to keep working when investors want to get defensive. 4) Cisco ( CSCO ) has been a relative laggard, and reality is there are plenty of tailwinds here across its core campus product with a refresh cycle, along with tailwinds on the optics and Silicon One side. 5) Motorola Solutions ( MSI ) role in delivering mission critical solutions to public safety agencies provides the company with a macro-resistant (non-AI dependent) business model while Silvus/D-Fend align the company with new growth vectors." -EvercoreISI analyst Amit Daryanani

"I've known President Trump a long time. We used to have quite a friendly relationship 24 years ago. We'd play golf," Clinton said (1).

And there was one idea Trump kept bringing up.

Economists generally view tariffs as a double-edged sword.

This can lead to inflation, eroding household purchasing power and raising the cost of living.

Shoppers are already seeing some of those costs at checkout. In an April analysis, Federal Reserve researchers estimated (2) that tariffs imposed through November 2025 had raised core goods prices by 3.1% by February 2026. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk added in a separate X post early Wednesday.

Americans have grown wary of the push to rapidly build new data centers over the past year amid concerns about the impact on energy costs and the environment.

articles.title: The fight for tech accountability starts now
articles.summary: A midterms rout for Republicans opens up an opportunity to break up the AI and tech industry’s cozy relationship with President Donald Trump.
articles.body: When Donald Trump began his second term as president, Silicon Valley gratefully embraced moral nihilism. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and more collectively donated millions to Trump’s inauguration fund to ensure his favor in a new era of gangster tech regulation. Meta overhauled its content policy to allow calling gay people mentally ill and women property. Elon Musk started throwing Nazi salutes — yes, allegedly, but he would soon be posting nonstop about protecting the white race from extinction, so that’s the most fragile of fig leafs. As of mere months ago, this was working out pretty well for them. The Trump administration took a mostly hands-off regulatory approach, particularly in the burgeoning field of AI. It decided to simply not enforce a divest-or-ban law against TikTok (something that was originally Trump’s own idea!), leading TikTok to thank Trump by name in its app. A Republican-led Congress was too dysfunctional to pass the tech regulations it did want. The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission still pursued some existing Big Tech lawsuits, but the flood of high-profile investigations we saw under the Biden administration — and the first Trump administration — slowed markedly. Musk functionally ran the US government for a few months. And beyond simple regulatory favors, Trump, once a vituperative critic of Big Tech, became joined at the hip with it. Tech CEOs prominently attended his inauguration, and their companies showered him with ballroom donations and gold gewgaws. The White House hosted the reveal of the Stargate Project, OpenAI’s massive data center plan. The US Army created a special detachment for executives from Meta, Palantir, OpenAI, and Thinking Machines Lab, and Trump tapped tech leaders as advisers. He ordered an entire technology renamed because he thought it would make the AI industry look better, and the industry duly fell in line. Now, these companies’ all-in support is looking awfully risky. Yesterday’s midterm elections were a historic disaster for Republicans. Democrats not only won the House and Senate, they flipped seats that were considered long shots or downright impossible six months ago: Texas has a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor. Trump is still president, but in Congress, Democrats will be empowered to launch investigations and haul tech execs into hearings, and they’ll have leverage to negotiate over budget and defense bills. And the electoral backlash, of course, bodes ill for Republicans’ prospects of holding the presidency in 2028. Americans are angry. Trump and his administration’s actions invited much of that anger: his pointless trade wars, a senseless actual war, adviser Stephen Miller’s brutal and lawless immigration crackdowns, and much more. But the tech industry is an easy target, too. Its hyperscale data centers became a flashpoint in numerous midterm races, and public trepidation about AI — a technology whose defenders argue it will destroy countless jobs and possibly kill everyone — is high. There’s a lot of dirt for newly empowered Democratic lawmakers to investigate. Google may strenuously deny a specious $24.5 million legal settlement was a bribe, for instance, but even as the minority party, Democrats rightly raised questions about it. Trump has enriched himself through connections with the cryptocurrency industry and in the process backed off investigating crypto fraud. Musk may have benefited financially in countless ways from his ties to Trump, and that’s on top of his reckless, destructive, and allegedly illegal actions with DOGE, which devastated parts of the federal government and likely led to hundreds of thousands of deaths. But tech is so overdue for a reckoning that the very term “reckoning” has started to feel like a joke. AI companies have been making vague “please regulate us” overtures for years, and it’s time to take their incessant doom-bragging seriously — by, for instance, using subpoena powers to push them on their responsibility for “rogue” AI agent hacks. Actual legislation likely won’t happen with Trump in office, but if there’s private information that suggests companies should bear legal liability, congressional investigations can help dig it up. The fight over data centers so far has mostly taken place at a local level, and newly elected Democrats at the state level will likely keep the pushback high. Given how many Republicans hate hyperscale centers too, a Democratic majority could also make a serious bid for federal action — at the very least, they could put a bill on Trump’s desk and force him to own his unpopular pro-data-center stance by vetoing it. And far more easily, they can stymie Trump’s push to override local regulations. Trump’s long-favored state AI law moratorium, which Republicans have tried to sneak through Congress multiple times, seems gone for good. Democrats shouldn’t replicate Republicans’ bad-faith attacks on the tech industry during the Biden administration, which saw Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) weaponize congressional committee powers to accuse social media platforms of censorship. But they shouldn’t be afraid to crack open the alliance between a lawless, grift-friendly administration and a powerful industry that paid him handsomely and was rewarded with regulatory favor. They’re also poised to figure out just how much Trump and his administration — where figures like FCC chair Brendan Carr display contempt for basic constitutional rights, to a point even some Republicans can’t support — have threatened that industry with punishment if it didn’t support him. Unfortunately, even with an undeniable mandate for change, there’s a huge risk that lawmakers will deliver exactly what they have for the past decade in tech reform: almost nothing. Despite the best efforts of some reformers in Congress, the US has perennially failed to pass even laws with bipartisan support, like antitrust overhauls and a data privacy framework. Hauling tech execs into court creates good sound bites, but without any real action, it only cements the idea that the government is useless. Democrats probably will soon have tech execs courting them as well. Meta, the fairest-weather friend in Silicon Valley, appeared to be already hedging its bets before the election. They’ll be tempted to retreat into the friendly relationship they had with tech companies during the Obama and early Trump years. But it’s too late to go back. Even at its best, the tech industry needs a check on its power — and the past two years have shown it at its worst.

articles.title: From Rs 60,000 rent to Rs 75,000 monthly travel: Bengaluru couple’s expenses highlight the contrasting lifestyles of IT professionals and freshers

articles.body: In Bengaluru, a monthly budget of Rs 1.73 lakh may sound extraordinary to some young professionals, while for another household, even earning Rs 25,000 a month can mean carefully balancing rent, food and transport. That contrast has drawn attention after a Bengaluru couple, Shubhi and her husband, shared a breakdown of their household expenses on social media. Both are senior software engineers, and their monthly spending reportedly comes to around Rs 1.7 lakh. The figure includes everyday costs such as rent and groceries, but one category stands out: travel.The couple spends approximately Rs 9 lakh a year on trips. Averaged across 12 months, that comes to Rs 75,000 a month. It is a striking amount, especially when viewed alongside the starting salaries offered to many entry-level employees in the IT sector. Their account is not a picture of every Bengaluru household. Instead, it offers a glimpse of how differently two people working in the same city can experience its cost of living.Where does Rs 1.73 lakh go every month?The couple’s largest fixed expense is their home. They pay Rs 60,000 towards rent and maintenance, a figure that reflects their choice of locality and housing society. Groceries come next, at around Rs 13,000 to Rs 14,000 a month. Shubhi explained that a significant part of this budget goes towards high-protein food items such as whey protein, Greek yoghurt and paneer. These regular purchases can make a noticeable difference to the grocery bill.Household help costs another Rs 8,000, covering a cook and a maid. The couple also sets aside around Rs 10,000 for weekend outings. Petrol and cab rides account for approximately Rs 3,500, while shopping and miscellaneous expenses come to around Rs 3,000.Then comes travel, which changes the overall picture. The couple says it has been travelling together for the past two years and has tracked the cost of its trips. Based on the amount spent over that period, its average travel expenditure works out to roughly Rs 75,000 a month. Taken together, these categories bring the monthly spending to approximately Rs 1.72 lakh to Rs 1.74 lakh, depending on the grocery bill. That makes the reported figure of around Rs 1.73 lakh a reasonable estimate.Their approach to money: Tracking, without keeping scoreAlong with the expense breakdown, Shubhi shared how the couple manages its finances. They track their spending but do not maintain a running account of who owes whom. Their explanation was simple: they consider themselves permanent roommates, not flatmates. The couple also offered a practical suggestion for people who want to understand where their money goes. An elaborate budgeting system is not necessary, Shubhi said. A phone's Notes app or a basic Excel sheet can be enough to begin tracking expenses.For those who prefer dedicated tools, she mentioned apps such as Money Manager, Monefy, Wallet and Spendee, which offer free versions. Their travel budget, in particular, is based on actual spending over two years rather than a rough monthly guess. This distinction matters because holiday expenses are often uneven. One month may involve no trip, while another may include flights, accommodation and several days of spending. Averaging the annual cost makes it easier to compare travel with regular monthly bills.What the same city looks like on a fresher’s salaryThe contrast becomes clearer when the couple’s budget is placed alongside entry-level salaries in the IT industry. TCS lists a minimum annual CTC of Rs 3.4 lakh for its Ninja fresher category, while Infosys recruitment material for Systems Engineer Trainees in 2025 listed a package of Rs 3.6 lakh per annum. These are examples of specific entry-level roles, not salaries earned by every fresher or every IT employee. At those CTC levels, the annual package works out to roughly Rs 28,000 to Rs 30,000 a month before accounting for deductions and the difference between CTC and take-home pay. The amount credited to an employee's bank account can be lower and varies with the salary structure.Now consider the couple’s expenses. Their Rs 60,000 rent and maintenance bill is more than twice the monthly CTC equivalent of these entry-level packages. Their average travel spending of Rs 75,000 is higher still. Even the combined cost of groceries and household help, at around Rs 21,000 to Rs 22,000, can consume a substantial share of a fresher's monthly take-home salary. Housing costs add another layer to this comparison. According to Magicbricks' Q1 2026 rental data, the average monthly rent for a two-bedroom home in Bengaluru's popular localities was around Rs 40,900. However, rents differ considerably across neighbourhoods, property types and housing societies.One Bengaluru, many financial realitiesThe couple's account is a personal spending disclosure shared on social media. Their salaries have not been made public, and the figures have not been independently audited. It would therefore be misleading to treat their lifestyle as representative of all senior software engineers or to assume that every fresher earns the same amount. But the comparison highlights an important difference in financial capacity. For one household, travel can be planned as a regular part of the annual budget, with Rs 75,000 set aside each month on average. For another, a similar amount may represent several months of income.Both households may be navigating the same city's rent, traffic, food prices and everyday expenses. Yet their choices, priorities and room for savings can look very different. Shubhi's account also offers a reminder that understanding spending is not only about how much a person earns. It is about knowing where the money goes and deciding what matters most. For the couple, travel is clearly a major priority. For a young professional just starting out, paying rent and building savings may come first.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: Not even $200 million could help Elon Musk buy Texas
articles.summary: Elon Musk donated lavishly to Ken Paxton and Greg Abbott, but Democrats still won big in Texas.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic Texas senator-elect, not only managed to flip the state in yesterday’s midterms but prevailed in the most expensive Senate election to date. More than $573 million was spent on advertisements between Talarico, his Republican opponent Ken Paxton, and their aligned PACs. And a big chunk of that money came from just one man: Elon Musk. Musk reportedly spent more than $445 million supporting Republicans in the midterms, making him not only by far the biggest donor in the 2026 election cycle but also in American history. And most of his money was spent in Texas, his home state and the headquarters of both Tesla and SpaceX. Musk funneled more than $168 million to super PACs that supported Paxton; Musk’s own America PAC, to which he funneled $216 million, also spent $34.7 million of those funds in Texas. All told, that’s more than $200 million spent on a single state. But Musk’s millions couldn’t buy him an election. Talarico beat Paxton by more than 12 points, becoming Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1988. And the governor’s seat flipped, too: Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, another beneficiary of Musk’s largesse. The Democratic fantasy of a blue Texas finally became reality — and it happened despite the efforts of the world’s first trillionaire. [Media: More than a blue wave, the midterms were a bloodbath for Republicans, who underperformed nationally even in the states they won. Democrats’ victories across the country often came down to money. But in Texas, it didn’t happen in the way Musk hoped. Talarico framed the race as a “top versus bottom” struggle between the ultrarich and everyone else. Musk’s donations to Abbott and Paxton may have emphasized America’s wealth inequality at a time when many Americans are struggling to make ends meet under an economic crisis caused by inflation, tariffs, and the ongoing war against Iran — all the results of policy choices made by the current administration. It’s hard to imagine just how poorly Paxton would have performed without Musk’s money. Paxton’s campaign received just $22.3 million in direct donations, a paltry sum compared with the $146 million Talarico raised from voters. Paxton got a much-needed boost from Musk, who ensured that Texans were flooded with anti-Talarico ads. Those ads, however, didn’t focus on the issues that mattered most to voters. In Texas, anti-Talarico ads largely focused on culture war issues like transgender people, a fixation of Musk’s. (Musk is estranged from his oldest daughter, who is transgender, and he has described her as having been “killed” by the “woke mind virus.”) One Facebook ad that cost between $15,000 and $20,000 urged voters to “defeat Talarico and his radical trans agenda.” According to an analysis of America PAC’s spending by 19th News, the ad was one of dozens of anti-trans ads paid for by Musk. But Musk’s money was also a liability for Paxton, which is perhaps why the now-near-trillionaire chose to operate from behind the scenes this time around. Musk endorsed Paxton on X — claiming the “fate of Texas and America is at stake” in the election — but against all Musk’s instincts for public spectacle, he didn’t take on a surrogate role in the midterms, in Texas or elsewhere. There was no Musk-led rally, no onstage jumping, no chainsaw in sight. Instead, Talarico repeatedly emphasized the relationship between Paxton and Musk, suggesting that to vote for one man was to benefit the other. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” he said at a rally in El Paso in late October. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV screen, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black-and-white photos, that was Elon too.” Talarico’s comments may have drawn even more attention to Musk’s cozy relationship with Paxton, which appears to be mutually beneficial. Paxton, who’s served as Texas attorney general since 2015 — aside from a brief stint in 2023 when he was impeached — has launched several investigations into organizations that criticize or antagonize Musk, according to a recent Wired report. Paxton has repeatedly followed Musk’s lead. After Musk sued the progressive media site Media Matters, Paxton investigated the publication; when Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against an advertising federation, a Paxton probe followed. “Elon Musk wants our land,” Talarico said at his El Paso rally. “He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.” Beyond trying to buy a senator, Musk also tried to chip in for a governor. Though most of the money Musk spent in Texas went to Paxton, he also threw a few million to Abbott, with whom he also has a close relationship — so much so that Hinojosa sued to view all 1,400 pages of correspondence between the two. And Musk wasn’t the only tech executive to support Abbott. The Republican, who promised to make Texas the “epicenter” of AI development, also received $300,000 from Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown, as well as funds from several data center developers. [Media: Musk seems to sense that the political winds have shifted. Usually a prolific poster, Musk deleted a “Vote red early!” post from Election Day and barely had anything to say on X that night aside from a quip about putting data centers in space. The other states he threw money at hardly fared better. Democrats won in Ohio, where Musk’s America PAC spent $10.4 million, and Michigan, where he spent $9.8 million. The Republican party’s only real victory was in Florida, and they barely managed to eke out a victory there. The amount of money Musk spent on this election cycle is both staggering and unprecedented — and it’s also meaningless to him. Musk lost half a billion dollars in his failed bid to buy the midterms, an amount that adds up to less than half a percent of his net worth. It’s possible that his loss will signal that even the world’s richest man can’t bend the electorate to his will. But it’s just as likely that he’ll spend even more money next time.

articles.title: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.summary: Data center backlash became a driving theme of many battleground races, and the subject of dozens of ballot measures.
articles.body: Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry. Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures. And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development. It’s hard to draw a direct line from data center backlash to the election of any of these candidates, and there were still some races where candidates who favored more limited restrictions on data centers prevailed. Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who previously lauded development in Florida, was elected as governor, and Iowa’s Democratic Governor-elect Rob Sand opposed a moratorium that his challenger favored. But even these candidates were forced to engage on data center issues during their campaigns, and will be likely to face continued pressure to put at least some guardrails in place. Ballot measures Voters were faced with questions about data centers directly in 45 local ballot measures nationwide. As of Wednesday morning, according to a site compiled by Redbud Consulting, the results of 33 of those will restrict data center development. The Town of Wells, Maine, favored a 180-day moratorium on large data centers, backdated to mid-June 2026. Several cities in Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25MW. The City of El Dorado, Kansas, voted to ban data centers with peak electrical load over 10MW for 10 years. Texas Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa will take over the governor’s seat from Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, marking a major Democratic flip in a state with the second-highest number of planned data centers. Hinojosa supports a statewide moratorium on data center development, while Abbott took a more measured approach. He announced a new audit this summer on data centers that could slow new developments from connecting to the state energy grid, but has previously praised data center expansion in the state. In another major upset, Democratic State Rep. James Talarico flipped Texas blue in a landmark Senate victory against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Talarico and Paxton wanted to remove some tax exemptions for data centers, and to make them responsible for their own energy infrastructure-related costs. But Talarico also put an emphasis on the facilities’ environmental impact and ensuring they shared their profits with the public, while Paxton’s message focused on keeping Chinese tech out of data centers. Florida Republican congressman Byron Donalds won the governor’s seat over Democratic former congressman David Jolly. Donalds opposed an outright ban of data centers, while Jolly said he’d bar hyperscalers for a year beginning on day one in office. In Congress, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would make developers pay for their own energy and water needs. Donalds’ win was still closer than expected in a state that’s been a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News reported that Donalds had exactly 50 percent of the vote, with 99 percent of expected votes already counted, while Jolly had 48.7 percent, and the rest went to an Independent candidate. Pennsylvania Democratic incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro held onto his seat against Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Both Shapiro and Garrity toughened their stances against data centers as the race went on, despite previously touting their potential benefits to the state. Shapiro signed an executive order that barred nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and took proposals for AI data centers off the fast track. Garrity has said she supports a development pause of up to three years. Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown won back his former Senate seat from Republican incumbent Jon Husted, whom Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned this summer in a leaked memo that if data centers were blamed for Husted’s potential loss, it would make them seem poisonous to future candidates. Husted earlier helped install data center tax breaks as lieutenant governor, though he more recently introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act in Congress to force large data centers to cover their infrastructure upgrade and energy costs. Brown hammered Husted on the issue throughout the campaign, and while he hasn’t gone as far as to call for a moratorium, he’s said that developers shouldn’t get tax breaks or get a go-ahead without local input. Michigan Democrat and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race over Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was one of the earliest politicians to stake his position on data centers, and has called for a pause on new developments “until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers called for a one-year state moratorium this summer, but not a federal ban. As of Wednesday morning, NBC News had not yet called a House race between Democratic organizer William Lawrence and Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, but Lawrence held a lead with 92 percent of the vote in. Similar to El-Sayed, Lawrence stated his position on data centers early on, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new developments during his primary campaign. Barrett introduced legislation this summer to bar nondisclosure agreements for data center developments and give locals more control. Maine Democrat and former Maine State Senator Troy Jackson ousted Republican Sen. Susan Collins from her Senate seat. The state legislature passed what would have been the country’s first moratorium on data centers, had the governor not vetoed it. But polls show that opposition to data centers among Maine residents remained strong. Jackson supported a state moratorium on data centers, while Collins opposed such a measure but called for more local control and protection for energy ratepayers. Wisconsin Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won the governor’s race over Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. Neither Crowley nor Tiffany favored a moratorium on data centers, and have distanced themselves from previous support. Crowley won his primary over progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong, who supported a moratorium. Both Crowley and Tiffany said they wanted to end state tax subsidies for data centers though they’ve accused one another of flip-flopping their stances. Nevada Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford successfully flipped the governor’s seat from incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo, whom he’d branded “data center Joe.” Lombardo has previously made supportive comments about data centers, but more recently introduced an executive order making tax incentives contingent on data centers covering power costs and meeting certain environmental standards. Ford previously championed a 2015 data center tax-break bill, but said today’s data centers are different from those years ago, and now supports a pause on all tax breaks for new data centers. Georgia Democrat and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governor’s seat over Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Bottoms favored a moratorium on data centers to review environmental and cost effects, while Jackson preferred to leave decisions up to locals. Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs fought off a challenge from Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Both opposed a moratorium on data centers in favor of power and water use standards. Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes held onto her seat over a challenge from Republican state legislator Warren Petersen. Mayes took a more hardline view than her Democratic peer, Hobbs, by endorsing a state moratorium on data center development. Petersen opposed a moratorium, and said data centers are necessary for technology residents use every day. Iowa Democratic state auditor Rob Sand won the governor’s seat over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. Sand did not support a data center moratorium, which Lahn did. But both agreed on ending tax breaks for the developments. South Carolina Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews flipped South Carolina’s Senate seat blue in a race against Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who had taken over the seat after her brother Lindsey Graham died. Andrews supported a two-year data center moratorium, while Graham opposed a pause and got significant support from a super PAC allied with the data center industry.

articles.summary: A U.S. Marine died during a training incident in Okinawa, Japan, on Tuesday, the U.S. military announced Wednesday morning. articles.body:
A U.S. Marine died during a training incident in Okinawa, Japan, on Tuesday, the U.S. military announced Wednesday morning.

The unnamed Marine, who was with the 3rd Marine Division, was training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, a Marine Corps base located on the northeastern coast of Okinawa Prefecture.

The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation, the military said.

The Marine will not be named until 24 hours after the family of the service member has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement.

“We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine,” the division said.

Last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will collaborate with Japan in the probe of allegations that a U.S. Marine killed a woman in Okinawa.

Okinawa’s U.S. population is close to 80,000.

articles.title: Democrats eye Big Tech after midterm wins
articles.summary: Democrats are making commitments to make artificial intelligence regulation and the investigation of companies a key priority as they prepare to take control of the House and Senate after Tuesday night’s election sweep. Shortly after news broke that Democrats secured a House majority, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar (Texas) said his party “must make it a…
articles.body:
Democrats are making commitments to make artificial intelligence regulation and the investigation of companies a key priority as they prepare to take control of the House and Senate after Tuesday night’s election sweep.

Shortly after news broke that Democrats secured a House majority , Democratic Rep. Greg Casar (Texas) said his party “must make it a top priority to protect Americans’ jobs, freedom and lives from AI billionaires.”

“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” he continued. “Congress should investigate how these companies are putting the jobs, freedom, and lives of Americans at risk. And we should pass bills to protect people.”

The scrutiny from Democrats was largely expected given the lack of AI safety regulations and the industry’s working relationship with President Trump.

Casar pointed to the election spending by tech executives, writing, “Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires. Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks.”

In the upper chamber, Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) wrote in a post online that Big Tech executives are “going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

AI industry spending contributed to candidates on both sides of the aisle, though the shift of the typical left-leaning Silicon Valley the past two years made a lasting impression on Americans’ perceptions of these firms.

In a recent Politico poll , Americans were more likely to assume the executives heading up the largest tech firms are Republican, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who clashed with the Trump administration on AI safety earlier this year.

Several Democrats on Tuesday hinted at increased pressure on the tech firms before taking control of Congress.

Last month, Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Chris Van Hollen (Md.) released a 27-page report of a nearly yearlong probe into how the data centers powering AI could raise costs for consumers.
