articles.title: Why removing your data online may still leave your family exposed
articles.summary: Data broker opt-out forms may not protect your family. People search sites can still expose your info through a spouse's or parent's profile.
articles.body: You removed your information from data broker sites. You submitted the opt-out forms, did the work and maybe even felt good about it. Here's what you may have missed: Your family members' personal information could still be exposed. And because their profiles may point directly back to you, some of your information could remain accessible, too. That's the problem with approaching family data broker removal one person at a time. People-search sites often connect relatives through shared addresses, public records and family relationships. In fact, the Federal Trade Commission warns that even after you opt out, your information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates. Here's how those connections can leave your household exposed and what you can do about them. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES Your family is already connected in these databases Data broker profiles often contain more than one person's information. They can include family relationships that help connect individual records. Search for yourself on people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or Intelius. Depending on the site and available records, you may find a section identifying possible relatives or associates. That list could include your spouse, adult children, parents or people who once shared your address. Some connections may even be outdated or incorrect. For someone trying to learn about your household, those details can provide a starting point. Now consider what happens when you remove your own listing. Your name might disappear from the site's direct search results, but your spouse's profile could still identify you as a relative. Your parent's listing might include an address where you previously lived. As a result, removing one profile may leave behind information that points to the same person. How one remaining profile can expose your household Family connections can create privacy gaps in several ways. Here are three examples worth checking. Through a spouse Married couples often share address histories, property records and other identifying information. When one spouse removes a people-search listing, but the other remains visible, the remaining profile may still reveal their shared address, possible relatives and other household details. Some people-search reports may also include property ownership or estimated financial information, although the details vary by service. For a scammer, a spouse's publicly available information could provide another way to identify or contact someone whose direct listing has been removed. Through an older parent This is one of the scenarios that concerns me most. Many adults help their parents manage online accounts and avoid scams. Yet they may overlook the personal information already available through people-search sites. An older parent's profile could include previous addresses, relatives' names and other public-record details collected over many years. That information may help criminals make a scam sound more believable. Consider the grandparent scam. Someone calls an older adult, pretends to be a grandchild facing an emergency and demands money immediately. The FTC warns that scammers may already know personal details about their targets or the family members they impersonate. Reducing publicly available information can remove some of the details criminals might use to support their stories. Through an adult child The reverse can happen, too. Parents may remove their own information without checking whether their adult children have searchable profiles. A young adult's address history, voter registration information or other public records may contribute to people-search listings. Those listings can also identify possible relatives. Someone searching for that adult child could potentially discover connections to their parents and other family members. For example, a scammer might use a child's name and location to make a fake emergency call to a parent sound more credible. That's why checking only one generation of your family may leave important privacy gaps. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? Why removing one profile may not be enough Data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records, publicly available online information and other data brokers. Even after a successful opt-out, some information can reappear when a site obtains updated records. Meanwhile, another people-search service may still have a copy of the same details. The FTC specifically warns that opting out of people-search sites does not remove the underlying information from government public records. It also recommends checking periodically for new listings. That's why I recommend taking a household approach to personal data removal rather than concentrating on one individual. How a family data removal service can help protect your household Manually removing personal information from data broker sites takes time. Doing it for multiple family members adds even more work, especially when you have to check whether profiles have returned. That's why I recommend considering a family data removal service that can manage the process for several household members at once. These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, depending on the provider. Some offer family plans that protect multiple people under one subscription. They can also send recurring removal requests when personal information reappears, helping maintain protection without requiring every family member to handle the process individually. Look for a service that provides ongoing removal requests, covers multiple family members and lets you track progress. While no service can erase every public record or guarantee complete removal from the internet, ongoing data removal can significantly reduce the amount of personal information available about your household. By protecting several family members together, you can help close privacy gaps that individual removals might leave behind. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. What a family privacy audit looks like Before you can reduce your household's exposure, you need to understand what information is already available. 1. Search for every adult family member With their knowledge and permission, search for each adult's name on several major people-search sites. Look at more than the primary profile. Check whether the listings identify relatives, current addresses or previous locations. Keep in mind that people-search databases can contain inaccurate information. A listed relationship does not automatically mean the connection is correct. 2. Pay attention to older relatives Check whether your parents or older family members have searchable profiles. If they need help, walk them through the available removal options or assist them with their permission. Pay particular attention to addresses, phone numbers and family relationships that could be useful in an impersonation scam. Also remind them to verify unexpected emergency calls by contacting family members through numbers they already know. 3. Check adult children's information separately Adult children may have their own people-search listings, even when they have never knowingly signed up for one. Check whether those profiles reveal current addresses, previous residences or connections to other family members. Then help them understand how to request removal and why they should check again later. 4. Use an ongoing data removal service After identifying exposed profiles, you can submit opt-out requests individually or use a service to manage the process. For households with several adults, I recommend considering a family data removal service that can protect multiple people under one subscription. These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, saving you the time and effort of handling each family member's information separately. Because listings can reappear, look for a service that offers recurring removal requests, ongoing monitoring and progress tracking. This helps reduce the amount of personal information that strangers and scammers can find about your family. The goal is to make it harder for someone to connect individual profiles and build a detailed picture of your household. Kurt's key takeaways I've talked a lot about removing personal information from data brokers, but there's another side to this that deserves more attention. You can spend hours cleaning up your own online profile and still have your name, address or family connections exposed through someone else's listing. That's what concerns me. Most people have no idea how much information about their families can be pieced together from publicly available records. I think protecting your household should be part of any serious privacy plan. Start by checking what information appears about your spouse, parents and adult children. If you find exposed details, take steps to remove them. I recommend using an ongoing data removal service, especially when you're trying to protect multiple family members. It can handle requests across hundreds of covered sites and keep checking for information that returns. You may never be able to erase every public record, but you can make it harder for strangers and scammers to put together a detailed profile of your family. articles.title: US Treasury Borrows Record $839 Billion in Single Week
articles.summary: The US government borrowed a record $839 billion in a single week via its sales of Treasury bills and notes — both to repay holders of maturing debt and to r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US government borrowed a record $839 billion in a single week via its sales of Treasury bills and notes — both to repay holders of maturing debt and to raise the additional capital needed to finance the federal deficit.

Auctions of bills, floating-rate notes and Treasuries due in two, five and seven years conducted from Oct. 26-30 eclipsed the previous weekly record of $795 billion, set in the same period a year ago, according to Tony Farren, managing director in rates sales and trading at Mischler Financial Group.

The $839 billion is the sum of the 11 auction sizes, and the majority of it went to repay holders of maturing bills. Only $68 billion represented new borrowing by the US government, and it's not close to record levels. Those were set in March and April 2020, when auction sizes surged to finance pandemic response measures, and weekly net new cash peaked at levels around $350 billion.

Gross weekly debt totals vary widely depending mainly on how much debt is slated to mature. This week's record total underscores how the accumulated debt — and the rising cost of financing it — is driving the US government toward ever-larger auction sizes.

"Nothing good is coming from Treasury gross weekly issuance at a record high," Farren said. "The No. 1 risk is that people are going to demand higher yields."

Over the past two years, the Treasury Department has met growth in its borrowing need by increasing the size of its weekly bill auctions, while maintaining the sizes of its seven monthly auctions of notes and bonds with maturities ranging from two to 30 years.

That will have to change eventually — or else risk bills growing as a share of the total debt, which exposes US taxpayers to rising interest rates because bills mature more frequently. Since early 2024, the Treasury's quarterly policy statements have said it expects to keep auction sizes steady "for at least the next several quarters." Bond market strategists expect that guidance to change when the next statement is made on Nov. 4.

(Corrects amount of previous record in second paragraph and new borrowing amount in third paragraph of story originally published on Oct. 30, before the release of the Treasury quarterly policy statement.)

articles.title: Hackers stole DreamHost customer files and inboxes during months-long attack | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The web host said hackers exploited a vulnerability to access customer emails and files during a "deliberate attack."
articles.body:
Web host DreamHost has confirmed that hackers stole customer emails and credentials during a months-long cyberattack on its systems. DreamHost disclosed the breach last Thursday after it sparked an outage that spanned several days, during which it reset some customer passwords.

In a data breach notice filed with California’s attorney general, the web host said the attack began in August and allowed hackers to obtain session tokens, which keep users logged in after entering their passwords. If stolen, hackers can break into a system as if they were that user. The company said hackers exploited an unspecified vulnerability in DreamHost’s file manager, which customers use to store their files.

When reached by TechCrunch, a DreamHost spokesperson declined to say why the company did not detect the cyberattack until last week, citing an ongoing investigation. The spokesperson did not say what the vulnerability is. The company said it was unrelated to the vulnerabilities recently discovered in the PHP web software .

DreamHost’s spokesperson said that the number of affected customers is “well under 10%” but would not provide a more accurate figure. The web host touts some 400,000 paying customers across its network.

articles.title: Prediction markets foresaw Democratic dominance in midterm elections
articles.summary: A dominant performance by Democrats in this week’s midterm elections created a political earthquake, shifting the balance of power in Washington, D.C., and offering a clear view of voter frustration with President Trump and his party. But most of Tuesday’s results were foretold in the hours before polls closed. Online prediction market platforms, such as Kalshi and Polymarket, have proven capable in recent…
articles.body:
A dominant performance by Democrats in this week’s midterm elections created a political earthquake, shifting the balance of power in Washington, D.C., and offering a clear view of voter frustration with President Trump and his party.

But most of Tuesday’s results were foretold in the hours before polls closed.

Online prediction market platforms, such as Kalshi and Polymarket, have proven capable in recent election cycles of providing an increasingly accurate view of the public’s perception of likely political outcomes and current events.

Prediction market platforms performed with impressive accuracy again on Tuesday, as traders poured billions of dollars into election markets at a time when the platforms face growing scrutiny from lawmakers about the dangers of insider trading and gambling addiction.

“There’s no way around it, the prediction markets seem to be highly accurate,” said Ross Dahlke, an expert in computational social sciences and a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

“The markets just react so quickly to new information in a way that a lot of traditional media isn’t set up to do, particularly with their concern over accuracy, fact-checking — for better or for worse,” he added.

Democrats were expected to perform well on Tuesday, given widespread voter concern about the economy and the war with Iran. But the volume of trading on prediction markets this election cycle and the speed with which the platforms were able to correctly predict races were notable.

Many of Tuesday’s key race results were being projected accurately on prediction market platforms hours before major TV networks, which use decision desk data and voter analysis to make race calls, declared winners.

Kalshi, one of the nation’s most widely used prediction market platforms, said Wednesday its markets had correctly predicted 98 percent of House, Senate, governor, attorney general, lieutenant governor and secretary of state races.

The company said it compared market favorites at 5 p.m. EST shortly before the first polls closed in Indiana and Kentucky to races that have been called so far.

Race results were still coming in on Wednesday, but Kalshi touted 95 percent accuracy on House races and 94 percent accuracy on Senate races, including highly competitive seats in Texas, Maine and Kansas that all went to Democrats.

Dahlke underscored that the initial numbers only include resolved markets, which may be easier to predict than those that remain unresolved, and that many races were fairly certain going into Election Day.

Polymarket said Wednesday its midterm markets were accurate in 98.4 percent of resolved races, when compared with the day before the election. It touted about 97 percent accuracy in Senate and governor races and 98.6 percent accuracy in House races.

“It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks,” Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what’s happening in real time.”

Prediction markets exploded in popularity following the 2024 election, a race where traders on both Kalshi and Polymarket correctly picked Trump to defeat former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Prediction markets have served as a venue for users to wager on the outcome of specific real-time events, from major business transactions and natural disasters to military actions, in addition to live sports events.

Lawmakers in Congress have voiced heightened concern about the ability of people with access to pertinent information on current events to profit from that knowledge using prediction markets.

Trading volume on Kalshi election markets nearly doubled over the past two years, rising from $1.3 billion in the 2024 cycle to $2.5 billion this cycle, the company said Wednesday.

A recent Washington Post analysis estimated nearly $2 billion was wagered on Tuesday’s midterm elections on platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket.

Despite recent successes, prediction markets have had some high-profile misses in other elections.

Polymarket showed Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro with a greater than 80 percent chance of winning late last month, before he lost to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

In the primary race for Los Angeles mayor, Kalshi traders were pricing in a 78 percent chance that Republican Spencer Pratt would advance to the general election. Instead, sitting Mayor Karen Bass (D) and progressive Nithya Raman faced off in the final contest.

And progressive Francesca Hong appeared steeply favored to win the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor in August, with a 95 percent chance on Kalshi, but David Crowley ultimately won the nomination instead.

Some observers saw Tuesday’s midterms as a key moment for the prediction market industry, both in terms of growing its customer base and its effort to fend off increasing scrutiny.

“This creates a powerful incentive to participate again, potentially converting casual observers into active traders. For platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, this election may have introduced an entirely new customer base that now believes it has an informational advantage,” said Matthew Bakowicz, a professor of business at American University.

“As these platforms attract more participants and larger amounts of money, lawmakers will likely focus increasingly on market integrity. Interestingly, the more successful these platforms become, the more scrutiny they may attract.”

articles.title: Man arrested near White House for making ‘finger gun’ gesture at National Guard
articles.summary: A man was released from custody in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday after being arrested just days earlier for allegedly making a “finger gun” gesture at a National Guard member near the White House. According to Monday’s arrest affidavit, 28-year-old William Clark reportedly made “a shooting gesture with a finger gun” toward a van that a…
articles.body:
A man was released from custody in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday after being arrested just days earlier for allegedly making a “finger gun” gesture at a National Guard member near the White House.

According to Monday’s arrest affidavit, 28-year-old William Clark reportedly made “a shooting gesture with a finger gun” toward a van that a uniformed guard member was driving on a street lining the Ellipse. The service member and other nearby troops then detained Clark before D.C. Metropolitan Police Department officers arrived on scene.

Metro Police arrested Clark for “threats in a menacing manner and assault on a police officer,” according to the affidavit.

A Tuesday court filing shows he was charged with “assault or threatened assault in a menacing manner,” which is a misdemeanor, but does not mention any separate charges for assault against a law enforcement officer.

The “threatened assault in a menacing manner” charge carries a maximum sentence of up to 180 days in prison or an $1,000 fine, per D.C. law.

The National Guard has had a presence in the nation’s capital for more than a year, though guard members were recently deployed to at least seven states during the midterm elections — primarily for monitoring ballot boxes and assisting in election security efforts.

Their presence at the polls and in Washington has not gone over well with local officials or Democratic lawmakers, who have said the deployment is unnecessary, costly and lacking a clear strategy. Critics have also rejected President Trump’s argument that the National Guard has significantly reduced crime in the capital, arguing guard members can’t make arrests and haven’t been stationed in high crime areas.

A guard official previously confirmed to The Hill that the Pentagon is expected to keep National Guard troops in Washington until Inauguration Day 2029.

In October, one guard member was shot in the leg while trying to break up a fight in Washington. Last year, two more were shot blocks away from the White House, killing one and critically wounding the other.

articles.title: 3M settles ‘forever chemical’ personal injury claims for $7B
articles.summary: Manufacturing giant 3M has agreed to a $7.35 billion settlement over personal injury claims related to its manufacture of “forever chemicals” used in firefighting foam. The settlement comes as the company has faced thousands of lawsuits over these chemicals, which have been linked to health issues including cancer and problems related to the immune system,…
articles.body:
Manufacturing giant 3M has agreed to a $7.35 billion settlement over personal injury claims related to its manufacture of “forever chemicals” used in firefighting foam.

The settlement comes as the company has faced thousands of lawsuits over these chemicals, which have been linked to health issues including cancer and problems related to the immune system, thyroid and fertility.

Forever chemicals is the nickname for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also called PFAS, because they linger in the environment for hundreds or thousands of years instead of breaking down.

One major application of these chemicals has been military-grade firefighting foam, use of which has led to significant environmental pollution .

Many lawsuits related to the firefighting foam have been consolidated into what’s called multidistrict litigation.

3M said this week that it expects the settlement will cover between 115,000 and 120,000 plaintiffs and address 99 percent of personal injury claims.

The company separately settled claims from public water systems for more than $10 billion in 2023.

3M Chair and CEO William Brown said in a statement the settlement is “a significant milestone for 3M and substantially reduces litigation uncertainty.”

“Following our 2023 resolution with U.S. public water suppliers and our more recent settlement with the State of New Jersey, this is another important step in managing legacy PFAS matters,” Brown added.

Meanwhile, attorneys for people who sued the company said this week’s settlement represented accountability.

“For the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade, 3M’s $7.35 billion settlement is welcome news,” Motley Rice attorneys Fred Thompson and David Hoyle said in a written statement.

They called the outcome a “favorable result for victims who are in urgent need of support to cover the mounting medical bills and other costs frequently associated with toxic PFAS exposure.”

articles.body:
The blame game: Vance, Trump point fingers at Iran after GOP midterm loss

President Trump and Vice President Vance have both blamed the ongoing Iran war for the Republican Party’s abysmal results in the midterm elections, brushing off other issues that appeared to tank GOP candidates.

“ The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy social media post.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he continued.

“But everyone knows why we lost . And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

President Trump earlier had partially blamed the Iran war for the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses , even as he stood defiant and said he would have done it again .

Later on Tuesday Trump said he knew the war would impact voting but “whether it impacted it or not Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Administration officials have quickly sought to deflect blame for Republicans’ trouncing, the likes of which has not been seen by either party in a midterm election in the last 50 years. The results are widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s presidency .

The war has sent gas and diesel prices soaring in the U.S. and globally since it began in late February, increasing voter frustrations after the president campaigned on ending foreign wars and lowering prices in 2024.

In pointing their fingers back at Trump , Republican lawmakers have said the war, the administration’s tariff policies, overfocusing on pet projects such as the White House ballroom and supporting weak candidates for the midterms ruined the GOP’s chances of keeping control of Congress.

articles.title: Licenciamento 2026: Uberaba tem 40% dos veículos sem o CRLV | G1
articles.standfirst: O licenciamento 2026 é exigido para todos os veículos a partir deste mês. Parte da frota está com débitos que impedem a emissão do documento.
articles.summary: O licenciamento 2026 é obrigatório e Uberaba tem 40% da frota irregular, sujeita a multa de R$ 293 e apreensão, com índices também altos em Araxá e Uberlândia.
articles.body:
Trânsito na avenida Guilherme Ferreira em Uberaba — Foto: Reprodução/TV Integração

Apesar de o licenciamento 2026 já ser obrigatório para todos os veículos desde o início deste mês, quase 40% da frota de Uberaba ainda apresenta pendências e não conseguiu emitir o novo Certificado de Registro e Licenciamento de Veículo (CRLV). O percentual de veículos irregulares na cidade supera a média de Minas Gerais, onde 27,9% da frota ainda não estava licenciada até o início de novembro.

Em Uberlândia, pouco mais de 23% da frota ainda tinha pendências para emissão do documento, enquanto em Araxá, o índice chega a 32,5%. Em Divinópolis, 27,6% dos veículos estão com pendências, patamar próximo da média registrada no estado.

O CRLV passou a ser obrigatório para todos os veículos a partir de 1º de novembro. Após o início do prazo, o Departamento Estadual de Trânsito de Minas Gerais (Detran-MG) apresentou levantamento na última terça-feira (3) apontando que 3.920.617 veículos ainda não estão licenciados para o exercício de 2026 no Estado.

Trânsito carros motos IPVA cidade Divinópolis — Foto: Prefeitura de Divinópolis/Divulgação

Uberaba e Araxá registraram um percentual maior que a média estadual. Na cidade do Triângulo Mineiro, até o dia 3 de novembro, 98.250 veículos não estavam licenciados, o equivalente a 38,9% da frota municipal, estimada em 252.505 veículos.

Em Araxá, dos 82.073 veículos registrados, 26.686 ainda não estão aptos para emitir o CRLV 2026. Isso representa 32,5% da frota da cidade.

O quadro é um pouco melhor em Uberlândia. Dos 469.547 veículos da frota tributável na cidade, 109.071 ainda não tinham quitado a taxa de licenciamento. Ou seja, mais de 23% estavam com pendência após o início da exigência da documentação.

Na região Centro-Oeste, Divinópolis estava com 45.531 veículos com o licenciamento de 2026 pendente. O índice corresponde a 27,6% da frota local, que é de 164.713 veículos.

Avenida Rondon Pacheco, em Uberlândia — Foto: Daniela Nogueira/G1

Caso sejam parados em blitzes ou fiscalizações de trânsito, os motoristas que estiverem sem o CRLV 2026 estão sujeitos a multas a partir de agora.

O Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB) estabelece que circular sem a documentação válida é infração gravíssima, o que resulta em aplicação de multa de R$ 293,47, sete pontos na Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) e remoção do veículo.

Desde o setembro do ano passado, os motoristas mineiros flagrados circulando sem o CRLV 2026 podem quitar os débitos via pix durante abordagens em blitz para evitar que o veículo seja removido ao pátio. A medida, entretanto, não anula a infração constatada e a aplicação de multa pela ausência do documento obrigatório.

articles.title: Hackers atacam banco francês e desviam cerca de R$ 615 milhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Dinheiro foi transferido para outros bancos e convertido em criptomoedas.
articles.summary: Dinheiro foi transferido para outros bancos e convertido em criptomoedas.
articles.body:
O banco regional francês Crédit Mutuel Arkéa informou na noite desta quarta-feira (4) que foi alvo de um ataque hacker estimado em cerca de 100 milhões de euros (R$ 615 milhões).

O ataque ocorreu menos de uma semana após a gigante das criptomoedas Binance ser alvo de uma ação semelhante.

O Ministério Público de Paris informou que abriu uma investigação formal após receber uma denúncia do banco, filial do gigante francês dos serviços financeiros Crédit Mutuel na Bretanha e em outras áreas do oeste da França. A investigação se concentra em um suposto ataque contra um sistema automatizado de processamento de dados especializados por uma organização criminosa.

O Arkéa informou que o "ataque sofisticado procedente do exterior" já foi controlado. Segundo o banco, os hackers acessaram a conta para fazer transferências para outros bancos, mas não as contas dos clientes, que não foram prejudicadas. O valor subtraído foi convertido em criptomoedas por meio de plataformas especializadas.

O banco não confirmou a cifra de 133 milhões de dólares em prejuízo divulgado pelo jornal Le Télégramme, mas indicou que essa é a magnitude dos recursos comprometidos. “A quantidade afetada pelo ataque, que está sendo avaliada, não é de magnitude suficiente para colocar em risco a saúde financeira e a solidez do grupo”, ressaltou.

A fraude foi revelada no começo da semana, por ZachXBT, analista independente especializado em rastrear fundos na blockchain, tecnologia que sustenta as transações com criptomoedas. Ele atua de forma anônima e afirmou que o valor adquirido foi canalizado por meio de contas abertas em plataformas de negociação de criptomoedas.

articles.title: Grocery store cyberattacks are ‘psychological warfare’ that could strike US, former FBI agent warns
articles.summary: Former FBI agent Nicole Parker warns that hackers turning up supermarket freezer temperatures in Europe could target U.S. critical infrastructure next.
articles.body: Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker warned that the next attack on Americans’ sense of security could come through the grocery aisle after suspected hackers have turned up supermarket freezer temperatures in Europe and fueled fears that everyday necessities could become weapons of "psychological warfare." Parker warned that cyberattacks targeting the systems people rely on for food and other essentials could also strike the United States. "Every human being has to eat," Parker told Fox News Digital. "This is the grocery store." HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT Her warning comes as the Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office works with the Defense Commissary Agency and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service to determine what caused refrigeration failures at military commissaries in August, an Army CID spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital. Investigators are also working with French law enforcement as they examine whether the U.S. failures could be linked to refrigeration outages in Europe. A cyberattack has not been established as the cause of the military commissary malfunctions. MAJOR US GROCERY CHAINS HIT BY CYBERSECURITY INCIDENT At least six commissaries, grocery stores on military bases serving military personnel, experienced refrigeration problems in late August. "ALL frozen food has spoiled," Fort Huachuca in Arizona said in an Aug. 26 Facebook post. FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS Other affected locations included F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island, Columbus Air Force Base in Mississippi and Travis Air Force Base and Fort Irwin in California. Fort Irwin limited commissary sales to dry goods after its malfunction. In at least one case, refrigeration units were set to higher temperatures overnight rather than simply shutting off, Reuters reported. HOW FOREIGN HACKERS COULD 'CRUMBLE' AMERICA BY TARGETING ONE ESSENTIAL UTILITY Separately, refrigeration systems at European supermarkets were disrupted Monday, forcing some retailers to discard food. Reuters reported that affected businesses included stores in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg, with temperatures in some systems reaching 122 degrees Fahrenheit. Parker said the incidents underscore a threat she has long discussed with former FBI colleagues: cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure. AMERICA'S NEXT WAR COULD REACH US SOIL, TOP ARMY GENERAL WARNS "What we're seeing right now is in Europe and other places, but it can very well happen on our soil," she said. She described the danger as "asymmetrical warfare" in which an attacker can disrupt daily life without firing a missile or sending troops onto a battlefield. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY "No one in law enforcement underestimates the harm that could be caused by a cyberattack against our country or against our allies," Parker said. The identity of those behind the European incidents remained unknown, Reuters reported Wednesday. Parker also cautioned against drawing conclusions about who was responsible. UKRAINE SAYS AIR ALERT SYSTEM HACKED AFTER FALSE RADIATION WARNING IN KYIV "Again, we don't know who did this," she said. For Parker, the potential damage goes beyond spoiled food. Targeting a basic necessity can also shake the public’s sense of security. IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC "This asymmetrical warfare has a very strong psychological impact, but we're Americans. We will not falter ever," she said. Parker said the response must extend beyond investigators tracking down hackers. Elected officials and local leaders responsible for keeping communities running need training and plans to help residents if essential services are disrupted. "We're in a place now where it's not just enough for law enforcement to be prepared," she said. City managers, mayors and city council members must understand potential threats and how they would take care of their communities, Parker said. She stressed the need to identify vulnerabilities and stop attacks before they happen. Parker urged families to keep basic supplies on hand and have a plan in case a cyberattack disrupts essential services. "I think if you are prepared, you do not have to fear," Parker said. She encouraged Americans to keep food, water and needed medicine on hand, gather important documents in a designated location and talk about how family members would communicate during a power outage. She also suggested having a battery-operated AM radio. "I'm not saying that, you know, you need to go buy everything off of the shelves," Parker said. Instead, she urged people to think about practical preparations as they go about their routines. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Parker, who lives in Florida, the approach is familiar. "We're used to hurricanes," she said. "The preparation would be very much the same." Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump's Fed pressure campaign hits a new Democratic wall in the Senate
articles.summary: That political firewall directly impacts the administration's ongoing effort to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook.
articles.body:
Democrats secured control of the Senate on Tuesday, a seismic shift that effectively blocks President Trump's campaign to reshape the Federal Reserve and neutralizes what many analysts viewed as a threat to the central bank's independence.

It also heightens the challenge for Trump should he maneuver to replace any sitting officials.

"Democrats' control of the Senate reclaims the party's ability to approve or deny the President's nominees for judges and heads of other executive branch agencies," Jonathan Pingle, an economist for UBS, wrote in a note. "That includes the need for Democrats to approve any new members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System should one of the existing governors step aside."

That political firewall directly impacts the administration's ongoing effort to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook. Trump fired Cook in August 2025, claiming she committed mortgage fraud by making misrepresentations on loan documents years before her appointment to the central bank. Cook, a Biden appointee, has denied any wrongdoing and sued. The lawsuit has gone through multiple court rungs before reaching the Supreme Court earlier this year.

Last month, Trump established a committee to determine whether her statements constituted legal "cause" for removal from the central bank, signaling that his efforts to oust her are continuing.

However, Tuesday's election significantly changed the stakes of that investigation. Michael Feroli, chief US economist for JPMorgan, noted that the Senate flip alters the math for the White House.

"Even a successful removal would not open a seat up to a friend of the administration," Feroli wrote in a client note.

Jaret Seiberg, analyst with TD Cowen, agreed that the inability to confirm a replacement may make Trump less inclined to fire Cook.

Not everyone is convinced the administration will back down, however. Loretta Mester, former head of the Cleveland Fed, told Yahoo Finance, "Perhaps it makes it less likely he will succeed, but I'm not convinced it will stop the president from trying."

More broadly, Democrats taking power in Congress changes the atmosphere in which Fed officials work to set monetary policy devoid of political influence.

Trump has been vocal and persistent in urging policymakers to lower interest rates. The central bank has held steady, raising rates at times despite the White House pressure. The new power dynamic gives them more cover.

articles.title: Voters fiercely reject data centers
articles.summary: Fierce pushback to data centers helped carry Democrats to victory in key races across the nation this week, and where the centers were explicitly on the ballot, they lost overwhelmingly. Midterm voters rejected industry-backed candidates and overwhelmingly backed resolutions to halt data center construction, dealing a major blow to the sector. Election Day marked perhaps…
articles.body:
Fierce pushback to data centers helped carry Democrats to victory in key races across the nation this week, and where the centers were explicitly on the ballot, they lost overwhelmingly.

Midterm voters rejected industry-backed candidates and overwhelmingly backed resolutions to halt data center construction, dealing a major blow to the sector.

Election Day marked perhaps the biggest test so far for data center sentiment. Technology watchdog groups are seizing on the outcome, stating results show the public is largely rejecting the facilities and the technology they power.

“Data centers represent a fear and an angst that voters have about being replaced by AI, losing their jobs, losing their livelihoods [and] the rising price of energy in their local area,” said Brendan Steinhauser, who managed Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) 2014 campaign and is now CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI. He added that they were also representative of “corruption” from “Big Tech oligarchs.”

While the economy, high costs at the pump , corruption and the state of democracy topped voters’ concerns , exit polls suggest data centers were one of several factors contributing to the blue tsunami Tuesday night.

In an NBC News exit poll , 23 percent of voters said data centers were “crucial” in their congressional vote, while another 33 percent said they were a “major” factor. Seventy-six percent said they would oppose construction of a new data center in their community.

“This is an issue that really defined affordability for folks, and governors, senators, House-elect members all saw it as a huge opportunity,” Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, told reporters.

Concerns around data centers were seen in several battleground races up and down the ballot, notably in Ohio and Texas.

League of Conservation Voters President Pete Maysmith pointed to the Ohio Senate contest, calling it “a really clear example where Jon Husted voted for massive tax giveaways — tax breaks for data center developers — and that was litigated extensively in that race, and it cost them, and it helped propel Sherrod Brown to winning that race.”

Earlier in the year, the National Republican Senatorial Committee had warned that data centers were an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

Further, Husted and several Republicans could not distance themselves from the antiregulatory stance of President Trump, who has backed data centers even as public opposition to them has grown.

Data centers are one of the only tangible representations of AI development, drawing backlash as part of a wider pushback on the technology. Seeing concerns around the facilities’ impact on local communities and the environment, several Democrats used data centers as a political weapon.

While Democrats coalesced around the issue about a year before the election, a growing number of Republicans, including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, abruptly switched their views as backlash grew.

Abbott lost the governor’s mansion to Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), and Paxton lost the open Senate seat to state Rep. James Talarico (D).

Abbott surprised the nation earlier this year when he said the state would stop issuing new permits for data centers. (Advocacy group Public Citizen found that some permits were still being issued despite the pledge, leading the state to shut down its automatic system .)

The announcement to halt permits came after the GOP governor previously stated that Texas would be the “epicenter of AI development” last year, before an immense swell in public backlash.

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa repeatedly hammered Abbott over his recent switch on data centers, calling his move to pause state data center permits “in name only.” She has vowed to establish a moratorium on data center construction, with her win Tuesday night throwing Texas’s data center build-out into uncertainty.

Steinhauser said he believes if Abbott had “come out earlier stronger, not only for a moratorium, but maybe for restrictions, holding Big Tech more accountable, he might have performed better.”

“But again, to lose by the amount of votes he’s losing by, it’d be hard for me to say that he would have won,” Steinhauser said.

For the industry, the Texas gubernatorial race could have significant consequences.

“For AI, the Hinojosa win is truly earth-shaking. The data center buildout is a Texas story, with only slight exaggeration,” former Democratic Rep. Brad Carson (Okla.) wrote on the social platform X . Carson is the president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a nonprofit pushing for AI safety guardrails.

Like other Democrats, Hinojosa took the populist approach toward data centers, tuning into voters’ sentiment about the ultrawealthy who may own the facilities.

Shaunna Thomas, the executive director of the populist, labor-backed super PAC Guardrails Alliance, said Tuesday’s results showed “data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues of our time as people across the country face noise pollution, rate hikes and Big Tech trying to steamroll local governments.”

“Americans of every political persuasion are sick and tired of the AI industry trying to control every aspect of our lives, building data centers in our communities, profiting off our data and trying to control who represents us in government,” Thomas told The Hill.

Out of 41 local ballot measures to restrict data center construction, voters were against the centers on all but one. Ohio, which is home to more than 200 data centers, accounted for 21 of these.

Dan Diorio, vice president of state policy and government affairs at the industry group Data Center Coalition, said in a statement the organization “looks forward to working with federal, state, and local policymakers, communities, and other stakeholders to earn trust, support responsible data center growth, and help build a stronger economic future for every American.”

Diorio added that the industry “will continue to engage with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities and ensure that the growth of digital infrastructure delivers clear benefits that communities across the nation are seeking.”

Still, many techno-optimists don’t agree that data centers played a large role in the election.

The election “was a referendum on Trump and his economy … efforts to try to deem it an Al election or a data center election are just wish-casting,” Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of the center-left tech policy group Chamber of Progress, told The Hill.

Chris Johnson, a GOP strategist focused on energy policy, said data centers were not the “most salient issue” this midterm cycle, but “it does get wrapped up as part of the affordability conversation especially as it relates to energy prices.”

However, Elon Musk, who reportedly poured at least $474 million into the midterms, appeared to acknowledge the facilities’ unpopularity in a post on X , writing, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: Iran strikes kept quiet during midterm homestretch set off worries about transparency
articles.summary: A series of reported secret U.S. military attacks carried out against Iran in the lead-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections is raising alarms around public transparency. The United States’s Monday strike on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz — including an antiaircraft facility on the strategic Qeshm Island — marked the latest in a series…
articles.body:
A series of reported secret U.S. military attacks carried out against Iran in the lead-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections is raising alarms around public transparency.

The United States’s Monday strike on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz — including an antiaircraft facility on the strategic Qeshm Island — marked the latest in a series of American attacks over the past few weeks, The Wall Street Journal first reported. The military operations have not been publicly acknowledged by the U.S. or Iran, and the Pentagon has not disclosed any bombing of Iranian targets since two days of strikes in early September.

President Trump on Tuesday insisted there was no return to fighting, calling the Monday attack “minor” rather than a return to all-out war, a message at odds with his insistence last month that Washington would “not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections.”

That, coupled with the Pentagon’s silence around a deeply unpopular war as Americans were set to head to the polls, calls into question exactly how much the government is obligated to disclose to the public about its military operations.

Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force judge advocate and now a law professor at Southwestern Law School, said there is no clear statutory requirement for the executive branch to publicly disclose discrete military operations.

During previous wars like those in Iraq and Afghanistan, the Pentagon held regular press briefings to keep the public informed, “a norm that has been greatly deviated from under [Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s] Pentagon, which has taken concrete steps to squash transparency,” she told The Hill.

One former Pentagon spokesperson had a far more blunt assessment, telling The Hill that the administration “bombed Qeshm Island during a news cycle where no one is going to cover this.” He pointed to the timing as falling less than a day before the midterms.

“To the extent that this is incredibly unpopular, they probably don’t want a lot of people talking about it,” the former spokesperson said. “The lack of disclosure raises real transparency concerns.”

U.S. Central Command, the military arm that oversees warfighters in the Middle East, did not respond to questions from The Hill on any recent U.S. strikes on Iran.

It’s unsurprising the Trump administration would look to tamp down potential coverage around the Iran war, a conflict that has stretched more than eight months, roiled global markets and sent fuel costs soaring with no relief in sight, with fuel prices proving a major consideration as Americans headed to the voting booth Tuesday.

Washington and Tehran have continued to exchange strikes since this summer but have not returned to the intense missile and drone barrages seen in the early stages of the conflict.

“I think it’s clear that the White House was trying to keep the conflict part of this Iran war quieter and not allow it at the near zero hour to hurt its electoral chances or become a factor in the domestic election more than it already was,” said Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute.

On Monday, Trump insisted the conflict in Iran is not a forever war, but a “soft war” that he could end at any time he chooses.

“We’re not fighting a war. … When was the last time we fired anything? This isn’t a war, this is a very soft war,” Trump told Fox News’s Sean Hannity shortly after the U.S. military struck Qeshm Island. “This is not much of a war, Sean, because there hasn’t been shooting for months.”

But following an astonishing GOP loss in the midterms, with Democrats taking back both the House and the Senate by unforeseen numbers, Vice President Vance on Wednesday broke his silence , saying: “The reason we lost is the war.”

Trump, meanwhile, told reporters Wednesday that he knew the war would impact voting, but “whether it impacted it or not, Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Public information on the war has dropped to all but a trickle, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declining to hold any press briefings on the matter since this spring. The Pentagon chief has been particularly hostile to reporters from legacy outlets — banishing them from the Pentagon’s hallways without an escort back in October 2025 — and any negative coverage surrounding the conflict.

The former Pentagon spokesperson said in a typical administration, for every kinetic strike the agency would release a statement shortly after the fact, and the current secretary of Defense generally would offer remarks about it, but there are no laws stipulating that must be the case.

“It’s not illegal to not do it,” the former spokesperson said of public disclosure. “Nixon bombed Cambodia and didn’t tell anybody about it for two days. It wasn’t a crime. But it’s just a thing that’s done.”

But they added that there are “no more norms of media engagement from the Pentagon. All that has gone away.”

As to what an administration is legally required to disclose, VanLandingham said there are overlapping requirements to inform certain members of Congress of certain operations, but not for general public disclosure.

The War Powers Resolution requires the president to provide periodic updates on the status, scope and duration of a war or deployment to Congress every six months, “but that’s about the only real statutory reporting requirement — after the initial report within 48 hours of initiation of hostilities or deployment into an area in which hostilities are imminent — for the war in general,” she said.

There are also several congressionally mandated provisions in the annual National Defense Authorization Act that require disclosure of U.S. military fatalities to family members.

“Accountability is impossible without transparency, and that’s the administration’s goal here — to avoid accountability for their wartime actions,” VanLandingham added.
