articles.title: Healthcare powers Democrats’ midterm rout: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Voters offered a strong rebuke of the GOP health agenda on Tuesday night as Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, with voters largely rejecting Republicans who pushed sweeping healthcare cuts. Here are four takeaways from the results. Health affordability was a winning message Democratic candidates made healthcare affordability a key part of…
articles.body:
Voters offered a strong rebuke of the GOP health agenda on Tuesday night as Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, with voters largely rejecting Republicans who pushed sweeping healthcare cuts .

Here are four takeaways from the results.

Health affordability was a winning message

Democratic candidates made healthcare affordability a key part of their messaging. They campaigned on restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and on delaying or rolling back the Medicaid cuts passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Polling over the past year consistently showed that voters are worried about the cost of healthcare — and trusted Democrats more to fix it. Democrats leaned into that message, and the results were borne out on Tuesday.

Ohio pediatrician and Gov.-elect Amy Acton (D), who led the state’s COVID-19 response, kept healthcare costs top of mind throughout her campaign.

She prioritized issues like forgiving medical debt, ending surprise billing and keeping Medicaid accessible.

“There is no more breathing room. From the grocery and gas bills, to the utilities, to childcare, to healthcare costs, Ohioans are doing everything right, but they just can’t get ahead,” Acton said in her victory speech.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health director of Detroit and Wayne County, made single-payer healthcare and a guarantee of care a central part of his campaign for Senate in Michigan.

“America’s greatness is the fight to guarantee all of us the healthcare we need if we get sick,” El-Sayed told his supporters during a victory speech late Tuesday night.

Democratic doctors and scientists rebuff RFK Jr.

Voters across the country chose physicians who ran diametrically against the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda and the Trump administration’s health policies.

Dr. Annie Andrews (D) in South Carolina made it known early on that her decision to run for office was spurred by the nomination of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to his role. Andrews has pledged to “lead the charge” to impeach and remove Kennedy.

“I’ve watched as insurance companies stood between sick children and the care that they need. I’ve seen how decisions made in Washington affect the lives of the children and families I’ve cared for, and that’s why I decided to run, because I believe we have a responsibility to leave our children something better than what we inherited,” Andrews said in her victory speech.

With El-Sayed and Andrews winning their respective races, the Senate will have Democratic doctors for the first time since former Sen. Ernest H. Gruening (D-Alaska) left office in 1969. And Andrews will be the first Democratic practicing physician in the upper chamber in nearly 90 years.

In the House, California pediatrician Richard Pan managed to flip the state’s 6th Congressional District and unseat incumbent Rep. Kevin Kiley (I). Pan ran on a campaign of holding the administration accountable for its healthcare policies.

The blue medical wave on Tuesday night was also a victory for 314 Action, the political action committee dedicated to getting Democrats in STEM elected.

“314 Action candidates flipped the House because this was a healthcare election, and we elect outsiders who voters trust,” 314 Action President Shaughnessy Naughton said in a statement. “Millions of Americans lost healthcare because of Trump, RFK Jr. and Republicans in Congress, and on Tuesday — voters answered by electing a new wave of doctors and scientists to Washington. This proves that STEM candidates are better positioned than any other candidate to win battleground races.”

Democrats will have major decisions ahead on healthcare, and party leaders will need to navigate the divisions between progressive factions that are itching to pursue “Medicare for All” and moderates who want more incremental change.

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like El-Sayed in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

“WHO WANTS MEDICARE FOR ALL?” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who won reelection, wrote on the social platform X late Tuesday.

During his victory speech Tuesday night, El-Sayed thanked his supporters in a call-and-response chant for backing “money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.”

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, advocates are looking to set the agenda with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election.

Neither House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) nor Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) — the likely Speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively — has endorsed the most recent version of Medicare for All.

But letting a bill come to the floor during the Trump presidency would catapult Medicare for All directly into the 2028 conversation and show Democrats no longer fear attacks about taking away people’s private insurance.

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a “single government plan.”

A national debate would likely include more details about costs and trade-offs that aren’t being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.

The same poll showed support plummeted when people heard the arguments that Medicare for All could lead to delays in medical tests and treatments and tax increases or threaten the current Medicare program.

But support grew when respondents heard that a national insurance plan could make health insurance “a right” or eliminate premiums and cost-sharing.

The alliance between supporters of Kennedy’s MAHA movement and Trump-aligned Republicans was already fraying in the run-up to Tuesday.

The results show that alliance may be on life support.

Conservatives and the Trump administration “broke almost every promise on MAHA, no new wars, Epstein, affordability… There is a clear direction of where conservatives need to head in 2028 if we want a fighting chance. Otherwise AOC will be president,” Turning Point USA commentator Alex Voetberg wrote on X late Tuesday.

Major MAHA-aligned Republican politicians in Iowa, Texas and Kansas lost, dealing a major blow to Kennedy and his allies in the movement.

The most significant defeat for Kennedy and the vaccine-skeptic wing of the MAHA movement came when Iowa GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn lost in a landslide to Democrat Rob Sand.

Kennedy and MAHA groups invested significant time and money promoting Lahn, who vowed to ban COVID-19 vaccines, end school vaccine mandates, clean Iowa’s water and regulate chemicals if elected.

During a MAHA rally late last week, Kennedy called Lahn’s race “the most important election going on in this country.”

Yet Sand also leaned into the environmental wing of MAHA and made tackling the environmental causes of cancer — and blaming “Big Ag” — a key part of his platform.

Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) lost his race in a major upset to Democrat Adam Hamilton. Marshall, chair of the Senate’s MAHA Caucus and a senior member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, has been key to shepherding Trump’s health nominees through Congress and giving MAHA priorities a legislative voice.

While some MAHA grassroots activists think the movement’s key principles should be nonpartisan, its leaders have aligned themselves with Trump and parts of the Republican Party. There have been months of infighting over the movement’s campaign strategy.

In his concession speech, Lahn said MAHA is a “real movement that has legs.”

“That says that corporate interests, lobbyists, career politicians, that we are putting them on notice tonight because the movement is just beginning here and now.”

articles.title: Chamber of Progress circulates tech ‘to-do list’ for Democrats
articles.summary: The center-left technology policy group Chamber of Progress is laying out its policy priorities for Democrats, as the party prepares to take back control of the House and Senate next year. In a memo sent Wednesday and first reported by The Hill, Chamber of Progress urges Democratic lawmakers to focus on consumer protection, economic opportunity…
articles.body:
The center-left technology policy group Chamber of Progress is laying out its policy priorities for Democrats, as the party prepares to take back control of the House and Senate next year.

In a memo sent Wednesday and first reported by The Hill, Chamber of Progress urges Democratic lawmakers to focus on consumer protection, economic opportunity and eliminating barriers to technology.

The memo, written by Koustubh KJ Bagchi, the group’s vice president of policy and government relations, was sent to Democratic leadership in both the House and Senate.

Recommendations include the passage of a national AI framework “combining public transparency, independent evaluation and enforceable safeguards” for advanced AI models.

Bagchi pointed to parts of New York’s RAISE Act, which requires large AI developers to publish their safety protocols and report safety incidents, along with California’s AI safety bill, S.B. 53. The latter bill established new transparency requirements for large AI labs, including mandated safety frameworks and transparency and safety incident reporting.

The memo also pointed to Illinois’s S.B. 315, which goes a step further than California and New York by mandating frontier labs with more than $500 million in revenue must submit third-party audits of their safety plans every year.

These bills were backed by AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic.

“Congress should require covered developers to publish safety frameworks, explain how they manage serious risks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers,” Bagchi said. “Obligations should be proportional to risk and developer scale, with protections for sensitive information.”

This framework would build on the Frontier Act, introduced by Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), which would create tiered requirements for AI developers.

Despite lawmakers’ increased talk around AI safety, close to no regulations passed Congress the past two years.

Democrats, who won in seismic numbers Tuesday night, have signaled they plan to hammer Big Tech over their business structures, but also through strict guardrails on the technology’s development.

Chamber of Progress, which often backs so-called pro-innovation policy, is also urging Democrats to put pressure on data centers to pay their own way, while ensuring faster approvals for the facilities that help power AI.

Democrats should also leverage fast-track approvals and federal funds for projects that are not dependent on local or state subsidies and ensure a return on investments, the group argued.

Data centers became a flash point in the midterms, stoking concerns over their impact on consumers’ utility bills and the environment.

Adam Kovacevich, the CEO and founder of Chamber of Progress, pushed back against suggestions the midterms were the “AI election” or “data center election” in a blog post Wednesday.

“The reality is that Democrats did well everywhere – not just where AI or data centers were an issue,” Kovacevich said. “Democratic governor candidates who did not support data center bans actually won at higher rates than those who did.”

Chamber of Progress is also focused on workforce and labor concerns around AI and recommended Democrats prioritize preparation for the workforce and educators.

“Democrats should help workers gain skills, enter careers, and maintain earnings as AI changes the labor markets,” Bagchi said.

The memo also touches on kids online safety, urging the passage of the Parents Over Platforms Act, which would require app stores to implement age-assurance processes. Age verification is heavily debated and has caused hurdles for other kids safety bills to pass Congress.

Other recommendations included action preventing predatory prices and reforming ride-share liability and insurance to prevent an increase in transportation costs.

“Congress should limit rideshare platforms’ vicarious liability based solely on connecting drivers and riders, while preserving liability for their own negligence or misconduct and existing insurance requirements,” Bagchi wrote.

articles.title: What the Midterm Election Results Mean for Your Money
articles.summary: Voters sent Washington a message about the economy. Here’s how the midterm results could affect your taxes, retirement, investments, housing and everyday pri...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Americans handed Democrats a thumping midterm victory on Tuesday, and with it, a mandate to fix their money problems. In survey after survey, voters voiced their anger over the state of the US economy, especially the cost of essentials like food, gas and housing.

Many voters now expect their newly elected leaders to do something to lower the cost of living and help them save. But it's rarely that simple. Congress can't control markets and GDP growth, much less gas prices and groceries. And while candidates have pledged to push back on tariffs and the Iran war, much still lies in President Donald Trump's control. Nevertheless, elections matter, and the results could have long-term consequences in areas like taxes, retirement, AI regulation and more. Here is what the reversal of power in Congress could mean for your personal balance sheet.

Trump's signature economic accomplishment was last year's passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Democrats won't be able to unwind the bill's major provisions, like tax cuts for high earners, since Trump has veto power over legislation. They could act to extend some of the OBBBA's temporary provisions that they favor, according to Alvina Lo, head of advice, planning and fiduciary services at BNY Wealth.

Those temporary provisions include deductions for a portion of overtime pay and tip income, as well as an additional deduction for taxpayers aged 65 and older. Also on the table is the status of the state and local tax, or SALT, deduction, which is set to revert from its current $40,000 cap to its prior level of $10,000 at the end of 2029. Some Democrats from high-tax states like New York and New Jersey have called for eliminating the SALT cap entirely.

Some state and local results may also have national implications. In California, voters appeared on track to defeat a tax on billionaire wealth and approved a measure making a higher marginal tax rate permanent. That suggests a broad wealth tax like the one floated by Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren and others is unlikely, Lo said, though there's an appetite at the state level to raise marginal tax rates. Those moves could give wealthy Americans continued reason to leave high-tax states. Those who can't move will likely keep setting up trusts in states considered tax-friendly, such as Delaware and Nevada, to reduce their state income tax, said Lo.
authors: Suzanne Woolley, Zijia Song and Prashant Gopal

articles.title: Tech is about to get hammered in Congress
articles.summary: Democratic control of both chambers of Congress will likely mean a new era of tech oversight and guardrails.
articles.body: Tech CEO hearings. Tougher AI and data center guardrails. Investigations of Elon Musk’s DOGE cuts. The gates are open for Democrats once they regain control of committee gavels come January after a historic win of majorities in both the House and Senate on Tuesday. “LAWYER UP,” the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee wrote on X in a message aimed at the Trump administration as well as “corporate corruption” shortly after networks like NBC News projected Democratic control of the House. “Subpoenas,” Senate Finance Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) posted. It’s clear tech executives will also be caught in Democrats’ crosshairs. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) posted in response to a comment that asked, “Live televised trials of Big Tech executives when?” Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX), chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and an Oversight member, made clear that AI companies are well within his sights. “AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” he said in a statement. “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.” Rep. Frank Pallone, the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, the clearinghouse for tech policy issues ranging from digital privacy to kids online safety to AI, pledged to advance policies that “protect consumers and the environment, prioritize clean energy, and rein in Big Tech.” Silicon Valley Congressman Ro Khanna said taxing billionaires should be among Democrats’ top goals. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has called to “PAUSE AI NOW.” Democrats have already used their position in the minority to signal what would be at the top of their committee agendas. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), for example, held a “shadow” hearing earlier this year after the Trump administration’s Justice Department settled its Live Nation-Ticketmaster antitrust trial, which state attorneys general who continued to litigate went on to win. At the time, Raskin told reporters that it was important to get a head start on administration oversight. “The corruption permeates the administration so much that we have to start building the record because it’s such an overwhelming task,” he said. “We will be using the products of all of these shadow hearings to figure out where to go.” More recently, Raskin demanded information from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle about nondisclosure agreements for public officials considering data center proposals. Democrats are also itching to investigate Tesla and SpaceX CEO Musk over all manner of issues. Musk spent record-breaking amounts trying to elect Republicans this cycle and held an unprecedented role in the second Trump administration as the public face of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), responsible for slashing federal jobs and eliminating the country’s soft diplomacy arm, USAID. Powerful Democratic lawmakers recently told Politico they’re eyeing issues like Musk’s role in DOGE, his alleged conflicts of interest, and his role in reportedly disrupting Starlink service to Ukraine. Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-CA), a lawmaker from Silicon Valley who just won reelection, says while he’s all for probing things like DOGE, he also doesn’t want his party to get lost in endless calls for tech CEOs to testify without significant legislating to back it up. “I think what is imperative for Democrats is to come to the table with solutions, not with slogans. Not with a lot of performative ranting, but actual solutions,” Liccardo tells The Verge in an interview. With full control of Congress by a significant margin, Democrats may be able to push forward legislation that would have otherwise been difficult to pass under current Republican leadership. They will still likely run into vetoes by President Donald Trump over things like more heavy-handed AI safeguards that the president has resisted. TD Cowen’s Washington Research Group wrote in a note Wednesday that it still firmly believes Trump “will veto any AI safety bill passed by Congress that would slow the AI model releases cycle.” The group also anticipates that Democrats will take another stab at tech antitrust legislation, which has been more or less on hold for years, but suspects those efforts will either stop short of a floor vote or get vetoed. Liccardo thinks AI safety rules should be at the top of Democrats’ tech agenda, followed closely by data centers and AI’s impact on jobs. Despite Trump’s aversion to many AI safeguards, he says Congress may be able to get Trump’s signature if they can muster enough bipartisan support. “Pushing Trump out of the way requires that we show strength,” Liccardo says. “We saw that in the past with, for example, the Epstein files.” When some Republicans broke away from him, Liccardo says, Trump realized “that he had to get out of the way of the train because he was not going to stop it.” Trump told The New York Times on election night he’d at least aim to work with Democrats, which could indicate a potential path for measures with a broad coalition of bipartisan support. The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), for example, passed overwhelmingly in the Senate in 2024, but was blocked by Republican leadership in the House. While Trump has not endorsed the Kids Online Safety Act, which was cosponsored by his ally Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), it’s conceivable it could pass the House if given the floor time, and Trump could consider signing it should it pass both chambers. “Big Tech’s lawless disregard for our children and our communities will be among my top priorities this Congress,” KOSA cosponsor Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said in a statement. “Whether it’s the industry trading kids’ lives for greater profits or its wealthiest leaders trying to buy influence from a corrupt Trump Administration, Big Tech’s reign of impunity must come to an end. Frankly, this issue has always been bipartisan, and I’m hopeful that I’ll have strong partners on both sides of the aisle as we pursue a strong oversight agenda.” Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) says Democrats should pass bills like those he’s introduced to make app stores responsible for imposing age requirements and keep kids under 16 off of social media to give parents back a sense of control. “Democrats should give voice to parents who feel powerless against social media corporations that treat their children like free labor for the dopamine economy,” he says in a statement. Data center developers are also likely to hit obstacles and have to slow their breakneck pace. “For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution…the answer in our view is a clear YES,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a note on Wednesday. “There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years. While Trump will likely veto any major draconian AI safety or regulatory laws, this will force the tech industry (Big Tech CEOs) to the negotiating table to try to come up with compromises around legislation in Congress surrounding AI related legislation.” Center-left tech policy coalition Chamber of Progress is already warning Democrats not to “confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate,” with CEO Adam Kovacevich saying that Democratic governor candidates who opposed data center bans won at higher rates than supporters. Liccardo says “it’s not a secret that data centers poll about as well as measles, mumps, and rubella, but I don’t think that’s what suddenly drove the midterms.” He hopes to leverage the data center buildout to make developers pay for needed investments in the energy grid. One company that could get a slightly warmer welcome in Congress may be Anthropic, which notably stood up to the Trump administration when the Pentagon demanded it agree to let it use Anthropic’s AI for domestic mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. The company is still likely to face many of the same questions and skepticism about its AI safety proposals as other leading AI companies, but its positioning over the past several months may help differentiate it from peers. Democrats’ recent messaging has promised a Big Tech and AI crackdown. Between 2020 and 2024, the party spent about $2 million to run six political ads that referenced keywords relating to the tech industry, according to public policy group Reset Tech; between 2025 and 2026, they ran 387, spending more than $100 million to do so. If the results from Tuesday are any indication, the rewards for following through with that message could be high.

articles.title: Security guard stops gunman who drove into Tampa-area Citibank Center and opened fire, killing an employee
articles.summary: A security guard stopped a gunman in an exchange of fire after the shooter crashed a car at the Citibank Center complex near Tampa and fatally shot a woman,...
articles.body:
A security guard stopped a gunman in an exchange of fire after the shooter crashed a car at the Citibank Center complex near Tampa and fatally shot a woman, later identified by the company as an employee, law enforcement said Wednesday.

The security guard was injured and at least four others were treated for non-life-threatening injuries following the lunchtime shooting, Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Frank Losat said.

"This was a tragic situation where a victim was killed by an individual who was intent on killing as many people as possible," Sheriff Chad Chronister said.

Thousands of employees were evacuated from the sprawling complex in the suburb of Brandon.

"My first instinct was to call my mother because I'm like, if something was to happen to me, someone has to know," said a cafeteria employee who requested anonymity because she works at the complex.

She said she sheltered in a room with five others until police arrived. Some cried, while others desperately tried to reach loved ones or texted coworkers for updates.

Losat did not provide details about a possible motive.

The first 911 calls started coming in at 12:11 p.m. about shots fired, and deputies responded to Tampa's Citibank office within one minute, according to the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office .

The gunman had driven over several medians and a grassy area, crashed through a fence and came to a stop in a courtyard where people were having lunch. The Citibank campus includes several three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant's employees, Losat said.

After he got out of the car, the man used a rifle and fatally shot a woman.

The Citibank security guard confronted the gunman in the cafeteria, where the two exchanged gunfire. The suspect was shot and transported to a local hospital, where he died, Losat said.

Body camera footage from 12:16 p.m., posted by the sheriff's office, shows an armed officer running across the campus. "Subject is in the cafeteria, possibly down," he shouts through ragged breath as others yell around him. "Shooter is down, shooter is down," he says moments later.

The video shows crowds shuffling through packed hallways to exit the building, their hands raised and sirens blaring around them.

"Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely," Losat said. "So, kudos to that security guard."

More than 300 law enforcement officers responded and evacuated more than 3,000 employees from the complex in two and a half hours, Losat said.

The victim was a Citi employee, said company chair and CEO Jane Fraser in a statement to CNN.

"My heart goes out to our colleague's loved ones, all our colleagues in Tampa and everyone affected by this horrific act of violence. I am grateful to the brave actions of our security team who prevented this awful day from being even worse," she said.

Citi's Tampa campus is secure and the company is adding security to its other sites as necessary, Fraser added.

Counseling and other resources are available for employees at the campus in the days ahead, Fraser said, while a company spokesperson told CNN employees are not expected to work Thursday.

Panicked employees took shelter during the shooting. At one point, while hiding with the others, the cafeteria worker said, a crying woman ran in, saying she believed the shooter had been close to where she was previously hiding. "I'm gonna die," the woman said she felt just moments before, according to the worker.

The worker said she recalled seeing people outside running and screaming, and seeing someone on the ground.

The cafeteria worker said she tried to stay calm and reassure her mother on the phone, and others in the room, that "we were going to be OK."

Doug Merritt said he was startled when his son called to say he had fled the Citibank building after hearing gunshots.

"He was very close to it," Merritt told The Associated Press. "He left all this stuff where he was at and he was able to get out of there."

Merritt said a poor internet connection made it difficult to reach his son, leaving him unsure for about an hour whether his son was safe.

"I wanted him to get to safety," he said. "I was upset."

CNN's Julia Vargas Jones, Isabel Rosales, Amanda Jackson and Devon M. Sayers contributed to this report.
